leads.title: Abraham smashes the idols
leads.summary: In Genesis Rabbah, Abraham smashes the idols in his father's shop, blames the largest one, and is thrown into a furnace by Nimrod. In the Quran, Abraham breaks the idols except the biggest, tells the people to ask them, and is thrown into a fire made cool.

leads.summary: Proverbs 22:17–24:22 closely parallels the Egyptian Instruction of Amenemope, including the 'thirty sayings' framing.

leads.title: The Buddha becomes a Christian saint
leads.summary: The life of the Buddha passed through Manichaean and Arabic versions (Bilawhar wa-Būdhāsf) into the Georgian Balavariani and the Greek Barlaam and Ioasaph. Josaphat became a saint in the Christian calendar.

evidence.text: The name chain bodhisattva → Būdhāsaf → Yūdāsaf → Iōasaph is the lexical spine of the lead.

leads.title: The raven that teaches burial
leads.summary: In the Quran a raven shows Cain how to bury Abel. In Pirqei de-Rabbi Eliezer a raven shows Adam and Eve.

passages.text: فَبَعَثَ ٱللَّهُ غُرَابًا يَبْحَثُ فِى ٱلْأَرْضِ لِيُرِيَهُۥ كَيْفَ يُوَٰرِى سَوْءَةَ أَخِيهِ قَالَ يَٰوَيْلَتَىٰٓ أَعَجَزْتُ أَنْ أَكُونَ مِثْلَ هَٰذَا ٱلْغُرَابِ فَأُوَٰرِىَ سَوْءَةَ أَخِى فَأَصْبَحَ مِنَ ٱلنَّٰدِمِينَ

evidence.text: Who learns from the raven differs (Cain vs. Adam). Dating PRE relative to the Quran is part of the question.

leads.title: Jesus brings clay birds to life
leads.summary: In the Infancy Gospel of Thomas the child Jesus shapes sparrows from clay and makes them fly. The Quran has Jesus fashion birds from clay that become birds by God's permission.

passages.text: (3:49) وَرَسُولًا إِلَىٰ بَنِىٓ إِسْرَٰٓءِيلَ أَنِّى قَدْ جِئْتُكُم بِـَٔايَةٍ مِّن رَّبِّكُمْ أَنِّىٓ أَخْلُقُ لَكُم مِّنَ ٱلطِّينِ كَهَيْـَٔةِ ٱلطَّيْرِ فَأَنفُخُ فِيهِ فَيَكُونُ طَيْرًۢا بِإِذْنِ ٱللَّهِ وَأُبْرِئُ ٱلْأَكْمَهَ وَٱلْأَبْرَصَ وَأُحْىِ ٱلْمَوْتَىٰ بِإِذْنِ ٱللَّهِ وَأُنَبِّئُكُم بِمَا تَأْكُلُونَ وَمَا تَدَّخِرُونَ فِى بُيُوتِكُمْ إِنَّ فِى ذَٰلِكَ لَءَايَةً لَّكُمْ إِن كُنتُم مُّؤْمِنِينَ (5:110) إِذْ قَالَ ٱللَّهُ يَٰعِيسَى ٱبْنَ مَرْيَمَ ٱذْكُرْ نِعْمَتِى عَلَيْكَ وَعَلَىٰ وَٰلِدَتِكَ إِذْ أَيَّدتُّكَ بِرُوحِ ٱلْقُدُسِ تُكَلِّمُ ٱلنَّاسَ فِى ٱلْمَهْدِ وَكَهْلًا وَإِذْ عَلَّمْتُكَ ٱلْكِتَٰبَ وَٱلْحِكْمَةَ وَٱلتَّوْرَىٰةَ وَٱلْإِنجِيلَ وَإِذْ تَخْلُقُ مِنَ ٱلطِّينِ كَهَيْـَٔةِ ٱلطَّيْرِ بِإِذْنِى فَتَنفُخُ فِيهَا فَتَكُونُ طَيْرًۢا بِإِذْنِى وَتُبْرِئُ ٱلْأَكْمَهَ وَٱلْأَبْرَصَ بِإِذْنِى وَإِذْ تُخْرِجُ ٱلْمَوْتَىٰ بِإِذْنِى وَإِذْ كَفَفْتُ بَنِىٓ إِسْرَٰٓءِيلَ عَنكَ إِذْ جِئْتَهُم بِٱلْبَيِّنَٰتِ فَقَالَ ٱلَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا۟ مِنْهُمْ إِنْ هَٰذَآ إِلَّا سِحْرٌ مُّبِينٌ

evidence.text: The Quran adds 'by God's permission' (bi-idhnī), which reframes the miracle theologically. That is a response-type detail.

leads.title: Dhul-Qarnayn and the Alexander legends
leads.summary: The Quran's Dhul-Qarnayn travels to where the sun sets and rises and builds a barrier against Gog and Magog. The Syriac Alexander Legend and the Alexander Romance have close parallels.

passages.text_omitted: longer than 12 verses; read it in the source

evidence.text: The Syriac Legend is often dated around 630 (Reinink), close to the Quran. The direction and the dating are both debated.

leads.title: Flood narratives across traditions
leads.summary: A divinely sent flood with a chosen survivor appears in Sumerian, Akkadian, Hebrew, Quranic, Vedic, Greek, and Chinese sources. The Near Eastern versions are historically linked; the others are candidate convergences.

passages.text_omitted: longer than 12 verses; read it in the source

passages.ref: Shujing; Mencius (Gun and Yu tame the flood)

evidence.text: Specificity test: the bird-release sequence (Gilgamesh XI; Genesis 8) is a rare motif combination that marks the Mesopotamian–Hebrew link. The Quran has no bird release.
Noah's drowned son (Quran 11:42–43) has no Genesis counterpart and is a sub-lead.
The Chinese story is about controlling the flood, not surviving it, so it is a weak match.

leads.title: Han Kitab: Islam in Neo-Confucian terms
leads.summary: Chinese Muslim scholars such as Wang Daiyu and Liu Zhi expressed tawḥīd with Neo-Confucian metaphysics: 真一 'the Real One', li and qi, and the Supreme Ultimate, in dialogue with Zhu Xi.

passages.ref: Zhu Xi, commentaries; Zhou Dunyi, Taijitu shuo

leads.title: haykal: the Sumerian 'big house'
leads.summary: Sumerian é-gal ('big house', palace) became Akkadian ekallu, Hebrew hêkhāl (palace, temple), Aramaic hêkhlā, and Arabic haykal.

evidence.text: haykal does not occur in the Quran; it is a control case for the lexical track.

leads.title: ʼâçôwn: a word shared by Joseph and Moses
leads.summary: אָסוֹן (ʼâçôwn, H611) occurs in 5 verses, all or nearly all inside two narratives: Joseph (3) and Moses (2). A rare word linking two stories.

passages.text: וְאֶת בִּנְיָמִין֙ אֲחִ֣י יוֹסֵ֔ף לֹא שָׁלַ֥ח יַעֲקֹ֖ב אֶת אֶחָ֑יו כִּ֣י אָמַ֔ר פֶּן יִקְרָאֶ֖נּוּ אָסֽוֹן
וַיֹּ֕אמֶר לֹֽא יֵרֵ֥ד בְּנִ֖י עִמָּכֶ֑ם כִּֽי אָחִ֨יו מֵ֜ת וְה֧וּא לְבַדּ֣וֹ נִשְׁאָ֗ר וּקְרָאָ֤הוּ אָסוֹן֙ בַּדֶּ֨רֶךְ֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר תֵּֽלְכוּ בָ֔הּ וְהוֹרַדְתֶּ֧ם אֶת שֵׂיבָתִ֛י בְּיָג֖וֹן שְׁאֽוֹלָה
וּלְקַחְתֶּ֧ם גַּם אֶת זֶ֛ה מֵעִ֥ם פָּנַ֖י וְקָרָ֣הוּ אָס֑וֹן וְהֽוֹרַדְתֶּ֧ם אֶת שֵׂיבָתִ֛י בְּרָעָ֖ה שְׁאֹֽלָה
וְכִֽי יִנָּצ֣וּ אֲנָשִׁ֗ים וְנָ֨גְפ֜וּ אִשָּׁ֤ה הָרָה֙ וְיָצְא֣וּ יְלָדֶ֔יהָ וְלֹ֥א יִהְיֶ֖ה אָס֑וֹן עָנ֣וֹשׁ יֵעָנֵ֗שׁ כַּֽאֲשֶׁ֨ר יָשִׁ֤ית עָלָיו֙ בַּ֣עַל הָֽאִשָּׁ֔ה וְנָתַ֖ן בִּפְלִלִֽים
וְאִם אָס֖וֹן יִהְיֶ֑ה וְנָתַתָּ֥ה נֶ֖פֶשׁ תַּ֥חַת נָֽפֶשׁ

leads.title: bᵉkîyrâh: a word shared by Jacob and Saul
leads.summary: בְּכִירָה (bᵉkîyrâh, H1067) occurs in 6 verses, all or nearly all inside two narratives: Jacob (1) and Saul (1). A rare word linking two stories.

passages.text: וַתֹּ֧אמֶר הַבְּכִירָ֛ה אֶל הַצְּעִירָ֖ה אָבִ֣ינוּ זָקֵ֑ן וְאִ֨ישׁ אֵ֤ין בָּאָ֨רֶץ֙ לָב֣וֹא עָלֵ֔ינוּ כְּדֶ֖רֶךְ כָּל הָאָֽרֶץ
וַתַּשְׁקֶ֧יןָ אֶת אֲבִיהֶ֛ן יַ֖יִן בַּלַּ֣יְלָה ה֑וּא וַתָּבֹ֤א הַבְּכִירָה֙ וַתִּשְׁכַּ֣ב אֶת אָבִ֔יהָ וְלֹֽא יָדַ֥ע בְּשִׁכְבָ֖הּ וּבְקׄוּמָֽהּ
וַֽיְהִי֙ מִֽמָּחֳרָ֔ת וַתֹּ֤אמֶר הַבְּכִירָה֙ אֶל הַצְּעִירָ֔ה הֵן שָׁכַ֥בְתִּי אֶ֖מֶשׁ אֶת אָבִ֑י נַשְׁקֶ֨נּוּ יַ֜יִן גַּם הַלַּ֗יְלָה וּבֹ֨אִי֙ שִׁכְבִ֣י עִמּ֔וֹ וּנְחַיֶּ֥ה מֵאָבִ֖ינוּ זָֽרַע
וַתֵּ֤לֶד הַבְּכִירָה֙ בֵּ֔ן וַתִּקְרָ֥א שְׁמ֖וֹ מוֹאָ֑ב ה֥וּא אֲבִֽי מוֹאָ֖ב עַד הַיּֽוֹם
וַיֹּ֣אמֶר לָבָ֔ן לֹא יֵעָשֶׂ֥ה כֵ֖ן בִּמְקוֹמֵ֑נוּ לָתֵ֥ת הַצְּעִירָ֖ה לִפְנֵ֥י הַבְּכִירָֽה
וַיִּֽהְיוּ֙ בְּנֵ֣י שָׁא֔וּל יוֹנָתָ֥ן וְיִשְׁוִ֖י וּמַלְכִּי שׁ֑וּעַ וְשֵׁם֙ שְׁתֵּ֣י בְנֹתָ֔יו שֵׁ֤ם הַבְּכִירָה֙ מֵרַ֔ב וְשֵׁ֥ם הַקְּטַנָּ֖ה מִיכַֽל

evidence.text: p = 6.2e-09 (hypergeometric, verse level). Counted from the original text with the OSHB lemmas (Strong's numbers).

leads.title: bᵉsôwrâh: a word shared by David and Elisha
leads.summary: בְּשׂוֹרָה (bᵉsôwrâh, H1309) occurs in 6 verses, all or nearly all inside two narratives: David (5) and Elisha (1). A rare word linking two stories.

passages.text: כִּ֣י הַמַּגִּיד֩ לִ֨י לֵאמֹ֜ר הִנֵּה מֵ֣ת שָׁא֗וּל וְהֽוּא הָיָ֤ה כִמְבַשֵּׂר֙ בְּעֵינָ֔יו וָאֹחֲזָ֣ה ב֔וֹ וָאֶהְרְגֵ֖הוּ בְּצִֽקְלָ֑ג אֲשֶׁ֥ר לְתִתִּי ל֖וֹ בְּשֹׂרָֽה
וַיֹּ֧אמֶר ל֣וֹ יוֹאָ֗ב לֹא֩ אִ֨ישׁ בְּשֹׂרָ֤ה אַתָּה֙ הַיּ֣וֹם הַזֶּ֔ה וּבִשַּׂרְתָּ֖ בְּי֣וֹם אַחֵ֑ר וְהַיּ֤וֹם הַזֶּה֙ לֹ֣א תְבַשֵּׂ֔ר כִּֽי על עַל כֵּ֥ן בֶּן הַמֶּ֖לֶךְ מֵֽת

וַיֹּ֨סֶף ע֜וֹד אֲחִימַ֤עַץ בֶּן צָדוֹק֙ וַיֹּ֣אמֶר אֶל יוֹאָ֔ב וִ֣יהִי מָ֔ה אָרֻֽצָה נָּ֥א גַם אָ֖נִי אַחֲרֵ֣י הַכּוּשִׁ֑י וַיֹּ֣אמֶר יוֹאָ֗ב לָֽמָּה זֶּ֞ה אַתָּ֥ה רָץ֙ בְּנִ֔י וּלְכָ֖ה אֵין בְּשׂוֹרָ֥ה מֹצֵֽאת
וַיִּקְרָ֤א הַצֹּפֶה֙ וַיַּגֵּ֣ד לַמֶּ֔לֶךְ וַיֹּ֣אמֶר הַמֶּ֔לֶךְ אִם לְבַדּ֖וֹ בְּשׂוֹרָ֣ה בְּפִ֑יו וַיֵּ֥לֶךְ הָל֖וֹךְ וְקָרֵֽב
וַיֹּ֨אמֶר֙ הַצֹּפֶ֔ה אֲנִ֤י רֹאֶה֙ אֶת מְרוּצַ֣ת הָרִאשׁ֔וֹן כִּמְרֻצַ֖ת אֲחִימַ֣עַץ בֶּן צָד֑וֹק וַיֹּ֤אמֶר הַמֶּ֨לֶךְ֙ אִֽישׁ ט֣וֹב זֶ֔ה וְאֶל בְּשׂוֹרָ֥ה טוֹבָ֖ה יָבֽוֹא

וַיֹּאמְרוּ֩ אִ֨ישׁ אֶל רֵעֵ֜הוּ לֹֽא כֵ֣ן אֲנַ֣חְנוּ עֹשִׂ֗ים הַיּ֤וֹם הַזֶּה֙ יוֹם בְּשֹׂרָ֣ה ה֔וּא וַאֲנַ֣חְנוּ מַחְשִׁ֗ים וְחִכִּ֛ינוּ עַד א֥וֹר הַבֹּ֖קֶר וּמְצָאָ֣נוּ עָו֑וֹן וְעַתָּה֙ לְכ֣וּ וְנָבֹ֔אָה וְנַגִּ֖ידָה בֵּ֥ית הַמֶּֽלֶךְ

leads.title: dâth: a word shared by Esther and Moses
leads.summary: דָּת (dâth, H1881) occurs in 21 verses, all or nearly all inside two narratives: Esther (19) and Moses (1). A rare word linking two stories.

passages.text: וַיֹּאמַ֗ר יְהוָ֞ה מִסִּינַ֥י בָּא֙ וְזָרַ֤ח מִשֵּׂעִיר֙ לָ֔מוֹ הוֹפִ֨יעַ֙ מֵהַ֣ר פָּארָ֔ן וְאָתָ֖ה מֵרִבְבֹ֣ת קֹ֑דֶשׁ מִֽימִינ֕וֹ אשדת אֵ֥שׁ דָּ֖ת לָֽמוֹ
וַֽיִּתְּנ֣וּ אֶת דָּתֵ֣י הַמֶּ֗לֶךְ לַאֲחַשְׁדַּרְפְּנֵי֙ הַמֶּ֔לֶךְ וּפַחֲו֖וֹת עֵ֣בֶר הַנָּהָ֑ר וְנִשְּׂא֥וּ אֶת הָעָ֖ם וְאֶת בֵּֽית הָאֱלֹהִֽים
וְהַשְּׁתִיָּ֥ה כַדָּ֖ת אֵ֣ין אֹנֵ֑ס כִּי כֵ֣ן יִסַּ֣ד הַמֶּ֗לֶךְ עַ֚ל כָּל רַ֣ב בֵּית֔וֹ לַעֲשׂ֖וֹת כִּרְצ֥וֹן אִישׁ וָאִֽישׁ
וַיֹּ֣אמֶר הַמֶּ֔לֶךְ לַחֲכָמִ֖ים יֹדְעֵ֣י הָֽעִתִּ֑ים כִּי כֵן֙ דְּבַ֣ר הַמֶּ֔לֶךְ לִפְנֵ֕י כָּל יֹדְעֵ֖י דָּ֥ת וָדִֽין
כְּדָת֙ מַֽה לַּעֲשׂ֔וֹת בַּמַּלְכָּ֖ה וַשְׁתִּ֑י עַ֣ל אֲשֶׁ֣ר לֹֽא עָשְׂתָ֗ה אֶֽת מַאֲמַר֙ הַמֶּ֣לֶךְ אֲחַשְׁוֵר֔וֹשׁ בְּיַ֖ד הַסָּרִיסִֽים

אִם עַל הַמֶּ֣לֶךְ ט֗וֹב יֵצֵ֤א דְבַר מַלְכוּת֙ מִלְּפָנָ֔יו וְיִכָּתֵ֛ב בְּדָתֵ֥י פָֽרַס וּמָדַ֖י וְלֹ֣א יַעֲב֑וֹר אֲשֶׁ֨ר לֹֽא תָב֜וֹא וַשְׁתִּ֗י לִפְנֵי֙ הַמֶּ֣לֶךְ אֲחַשְׁוֵר֔וֹשׁ וּמַלְכוּתָהּ֙ יִתֵּ֣ן הַמֶּ֔לֶךְ לִרְעוּתָ֖הּ הַטּוֹבָ֥ה מִמֶּֽנָּה

וַיְהִ֗י בְּהִשָּׁמַ֤ע דְּבַר הַמֶּ֨לֶךְ֙ וְדָת֔וֹ וּֽבְהִקָּבֵ֞ץ נְעָר֥וֹת רַבּ֛וֹת אֶל שׁוּשַׁ֥ן הַבִּירָ֖ה אֶל יַ֣ד הֵגָ֑י וַתִּלָּקַ֤ח אֶסְתֵּר֙ אֶל בֵּ֣ית הַמֶּ֔לֶךְ אֶל יַ֥ד הֵגַ֖י שֹׁמֵ֥ר הַנָּשִֽׁים

וּבְהַגִּ֡יעַ תֹּר֩ נַעֲרָ֨ה וְנַעֲרָ֜ה לָב֣וֹא אֶל הַמֶּ֣לֶךְ אֲחַשְׁוֵר֗וֹשׁ מִקֵּץ֩ הֱי֨וֹת לָ֜הּ כְּדָ֤ת הַנָּשִׁים֙ שְׁנֵ֣ים עָשָׂ֣ר חֹ֔דֶשׁ כִּ֛י כֵּ֥ן יִמְלְא֖וּ יְמֵ֣י מְרוּקֵיהֶ֑ן שִׁשָּׁ֤ה חֳדָשִׁים֙ בְּשֶׁ֣מֶן הַמֹּ֔ר וְשִׁשָּׁ֤ה חֳדָשִׁים֙ בַּבְּשָׂמִ֔ים וּבְתַמְרוּקֵ֖י הַנָּשִֽׁים

וַיֹּ֤אמֶר הָמָן֙ לַמֶּ֣לֶךְ אֲחַשְׁוֵר֔וֹשׁ יֶשְׁנ֣וֹ עַם אֶחָ֗ד מְפֻזָּ֤ר וּמְפֹרָד֙ בֵּ֣ין הָֽעַמִּ֔ים בְּכֹ֖ל מְדִינ֣וֹת מַלְכוּתֶ֑ךָ וְדָתֵיהֶ֞ם שֹׁנ֣וֹת מִכָּל עָ֗ם וְאֶת דָּתֵ֤י הַמֶּ֨לֶךְ֙ אֵינָ֣ם עֹשִׂ֔ים וְלַמֶּ֥לֶךְ אֵין שֹׁוֶ֖ה לְהַנִּיחָֽם
פַּתְשֶׁ֣גֶן הַכְּתָ֗ב לְהִנָּ֤תֵֽן דָּת֙ בְּכָל מְדִינָ֣ה וּמְדִינָ֔ה גָּל֖וּי לְכָל הָֽעַמִּ֑ים לִהְי֥וֹת עֲתִדִ֖ים לַיּ֥וֹם הַזֶּֽה
הָֽרָצִ֞ים יָצְא֤וּ דְחוּפִים֙ בִּדְבַ֣ר הַמֶּ֔לֶךְ וְהַדָּ֥ת נִתְּנָ֖ה בְּשׁוּשַׁ֣ן הַבִּירָ֑ה וְהַמֶּ֤לֶךְ וְהָמָן֙ יָשְׁב֣וּ לִשְׁתּ֔וֹת וְהָעִ֥יר שׁוּשָׁ֖ן נָבֽוֹכָה
וּבְכָל מְדִינָ֣ה וּמְדִינָ֗ה מְקוֹם֙ אֲשֶׁ֨ר דְּבַר הַמֶּ֤לֶךְ וְדָתוֹ֙ מַגִּ֔יעַ אֵ֤בֶל גָּדוֹל֙ לַיְּהוּדִ֔ים וְצ֥וֹם וּבְכִ֖י וּמִסְפֵּ֑ד שַׂ֣ק וָאֵ֔פֶר יֻצַּ֖ע לָֽרַבִּֽים

וְאֶת פַּתְשֶׁ֣גֶן כְּתָֽב הַ֠דָּת אֲשֶׁר נִתַּ֨ן בְּשׁוּשָׁ֤ן לְהַשְׁמִידָם֙ נָ֣תַן ל֔וֹ לְהַרְא֥וֹת אֶת אֶסְתֵּ֖ר וּלְהַגִּ֣יד לָ֑הּ וּלְצַוּ֣וֹת עָלֶ֗יהָ לָב֨וֹא אֶל הַמֶּ֧לֶךְ לְהִֽתְחַנֶּן ל֛וֹ וּלְבַקֵּ֥שׁ מִלְּפָנָ֖יו עַל עַמָּֽהּ

כָּל עַבְדֵ֣י הַמֶּ֡לֶךְ וְעַם מְדִינ֨וֹת הַמֶּ֜לֶךְ יֽוֹדְעִ֗ים אֲשֶׁ֣ר כָּל אִ֣ישׁ וְאִשָּׁ֡ה אֲשֶׁ֣ר יָבֽוֹא אֶל הַמֶּלֶךְ֩ אֶל הֶחָצֵ֨ר הַפְּנִימִ֜ית אֲשֶׁ֣ר לֹֽא יִקָּרֵ֗א אַחַ֤ת דָּתוֹ֙ לְהָמִ֔ית לְ֠בַד מֵאֲשֶׁ֨ר יֽוֹשִׁיט ל֥וֹ הַמֶּ֛לֶךְ אֶת שַׁרְבִ֥יט הַזָּהָ֖ב וְחָיָ֑ה וַאֲנִ֗י לֹ֤א נִקְרֵ֨אתי֙ לָב֣וֹא אֶל הַמֶּ֔לֶךְ זֶ֖ה שְׁלוֹשִׁ֥ים יֽוֹם

לֵךְ֩ כְּנ֨וֹס אֶת כָּל הַיְּהוּדִ֜ים הַֽנִּמְצְאִ֣ים בְּשׁוּשָׁ֗ן וְצ֣וּמוּ עָ֠לַי וְאַל תֹּאכְל֨וּ וְאַל תִּשְׁתּ֜וּ שְׁלֹ֤שֶׁת יָמִים֙ לַ֣יְלָה וָי֔וֹם גַּם אֲנִ֥י וְנַעֲרֹתַ֖י אָצ֣וּם כֵּ֑ן וּבְכֵ֞ן אָב֤וֹא אֶל הַמֶּ֨לֶךְ֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר לֹֽא כַדָּ֔ת וְכַאֲשֶׁ֥ר אָבַ֖דְתִּי אָבָֽדְתִּי

leads.title: malkâh: a word shared by Esther and Solomon
leads.summary: מַלְכָּה (malkâh, H4436) occurs in 34 verses, all or nearly all inside two narratives: Esther (24) and Solomon (8). A rare word linking two stories.

passages.text: וּמַֽלְכַּת שְׁבָ֗א שֹׁמַ֛עַת אֶת שֵׁ֥מַע שְׁלֹמֹ֖ה לְשֵׁ֣ם יְהוָ֑ה וַתָּבֹ֥א לְנַסֹּת֖וֹ בְּחִידֽוֹת
וַתֵּ֨רֶא֙ מַֽלְכַּת שְׁבָ֔א אֵ֖ת כָּל חָכְמַ֣ת שְׁלֹמֹ֑ה וְהַבַּ֖יִת אֲשֶׁ֥ר בָּנָֽה

וַתִּתֵּ֨ן לַמֶּ֜לֶךְ מֵאָ֥ה וְעֶשְׂרִ֣ים כִּכַּ֣ר זָהָ֗ב וּבְשָׂמִ֛ים הַרְבֵּ֥ה מְאֹ֖ד וְאֶ֣בֶן יְקָרָ֑ה לֹא בָא֩ כַבֹּ֨שֶׂם הַה֥וּא עוֹד֙ לָרֹ֔ב אֲשֶׁר נָתְנָ֥ה מַֽלְכַּת שְׁבָ֖א לַמֶּ֥לֶךְ שְׁלֹמֹֽה
וְהַמֶּ֨לֶךְ שְׁלֹמֹ֜ה נָתַ֣ן לְמַֽלְכַּת שְׁבָ֗א אֶת כָּל חֶפְצָהּ֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר שָׁאָ֔לָה מִלְּבַד֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר נָֽתַן לָ֔הּ כְּיַ֖ד הַמֶּ֣לֶךְ שְׁלֹמֹ֑ה וַתֵּ֛פֶן וַתֵּ֥לֶךְ לְאַרְצָ֖הּ הִ֥יא וַעֲבָדֶֽיהָ

וּמַֽלְכַּת שְׁבָ֗א שָֽׁמְעָה֮ אֶת שֵׁ֣מַע שְׁלֹמֹה֒ וַתָּב֣וֹא לְנַסּוֹת֩ אֶת שְׁלֹמֹ֨ה בְחִיד֜וֹת בִּירֽוּשָׁלִַ֗ם בְּחַ֣יִל כָּבֵ֣ד מְאֹ֡ד וּ֠גְמַלִּים נֹשְׂאִ֨ים בְּשָׂמִ֧ים וְזָהָ֛ב לָרֹ֖ב וְאֶ֣בֶן יְקָרָ֑ה וַתָּבוֹא֙ אֶל שְׁלֹמֹ֔ה וַתְּדַבֵּ֣ר עִמּ֔וֹ אֵ֛ת כָּל אֲשֶׁ֥ר הָיָ֖ה עִם לְבָבָֽהּ
וַתֵּ֨רֶא֙ מַֽלְכַּת שְׁבָ֔א אֵ֖ת חָכְמַ֣ת שְׁלֹמֹ֑ה וְהַבַּ֖יִת אֲשֶׁ֥ר בָּנָֽה
וַתִּתֵּ֨ן לַמֶּ֜לֶךְ מֵאָ֥ה וְעֶשְׂרִ֣ים כִּכַּ֣ר זָהָ֗ב וּבְשָׂמִ֛ים לָרֹ֥ב מְאֹ֖ד וְאֶ֣בֶן יְקָרָ֑ה וְלֹ֤א הָיָה֙ כַּבֹּ֣שֶׂם הַה֔וּא אֲשֶׁר נָתְנָ֥ה מַֽלְכַּת שְׁבָ֖א לַמֶּ֥לֶךְ שְׁלֹמֹֽה
וְהַמֶּ֨לֶךְ שְׁלֹמֹ֜ה נָתַ֣ן לְמַֽלְכַּת שְׁבָ֗א אֶת כָּל חֶפְצָהּ֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר שָׁאָ֔לָה מִלְּבַ֖ד אֲשֶׁר הֵבִ֣יאָה אֶל הַמֶּ֑לֶךְ וַֽתַּהֲפֹ֛ךְ וַתֵּ֥לֶךְ לְאַרְצָ֖הּ הִ֥יא וַעֲבָדֶֽיהָ
גַּ֚ם וַשְׁתִּ֣י הַמַּלְכָּ֔ה עָשְׂתָ֖ה מִשְׁתֵּ֣ה נָשִׁ֑ים בֵּ֚ית הַמַּלְכ֔וּת אֲשֶׁ֖ר לַמֶּ֥לֶךְ אֲחַשְׁוֵרֽוֹשׁ
לְ֠הָבִיא אֶת וַשְׁתִּ֧י הַמַּלְכָּ֛ה לִפְנֵ֥י הַמֶּ֖לֶךְ בְּכֶ֣תֶר מַלְכ֑וּת לְהַרְא֨וֹת הָֽעַמִּ֤ים וְהַשָּׂרִים֙ אֶת יָפְיָ֔הּ כִּֽי טוֹבַ֥ת מַרְאֶ֖ה הִֽיא
וַתְּמָאֵ֞ן הַמַּלְכָּ֣ה וַשְׁתִּ֗י לָבוֹא֙ בִּדְבַ֣ר הַמֶּ֔לֶךְ אֲשֶׁ֖ר בְּיַ֣ד הַסָּרִיסִ֑ים וַיִּקְצֹ֤ף הַמֶּ֨לֶךְ֙ מְאֹ֔ד וַחֲמָת֖וֹ בָּעֲרָ֥ה בֽוֹ
כְּדָת֙ מַֽה לַּעֲשׂ֔וֹת בַּמַּלְכָּ֖ה וַשְׁתִּ֑י עַ֣ל אֲשֶׁ֣ר לֹֽא עָשְׂתָ֗ה אֶֽת מַאֲמַר֙ הַמֶּ֣לֶךְ אֲחַשְׁוֵר֔וֹשׁ בְּיַ֖ד הַסָּרִיסִֽים

וַיֹּ֣אמֶר מומכן מְמוּכָ֗ן לִפְנֵ֤י הַמֶּ֨לֶךְ֙ וְהַשָּׂרִ֔ים לֹ֤א עַל הַמֶּ֨לֶךְ֙ לְבַדּ֔וֹ עָוְתָ֖ה וַשְׁתִּ֣י הַמַּלְכָּ֑ה כִּ֤י עַל כָּל הַשָּׂרִים֙ וְעַל כָּל הָ֣עַמִּ֔ים אֲשֶׁ֕ר בְּכָל מְדִינ֖וֹת הַמֶּ֥לֶךְ אֲחַשְׁוֵרֽוֹשׁ
כִּֽי יֵצֵ֤א דְבַר הַמַּלְכָּה֙ עַל כָּל הַנָּשִׁ֔ים לְהַבְז֥וֹת בַּעְלֵיהֶ֖ן בְּעֵינֵיהֶ֑ן בְּאָמְרָ֗ם הַמֶּ֣לֶךְ אֲחַשְׁוֵר֡וֹשׁ אָמַ֞ר לְהָבִ֨יא אֶת וַשְׁתִּ֧י הַמַּלְכָּ֛ה לְפָנָ֖יו וְלֹא בָֽאָה
וְֽהַיּ֨וֹם הַזֶּ֜ה תֹּאמַ֣רְנָה שָׂר֣וֹת פָּֽרַס וּמָדַ֗י אֲשֶׁ֤ר שָֽׁמְעוּ֙ אֶת דְּבַ֣ר הַמַּלְכָּ֔ה לְכֹ֖ל שָׂרֵ֣י הַמֶּ֑לֶךְ וּכְדַ֖י בִּזָּי֥וֹן וָקָֽצֶף

leads.title: millâh: a word shared by David and Job
leads.summary: מִלָּה (millâh, H4405) occurs in 38 verses, all or nearly all inside two narratives: David (1) and Job (34). A rare word linking two stories.

passages.text: ר֥וּחַ יְהוָ֖ה דִּבֶּר בִּ֑י וּמִלָּת֖וֹ עַל לְשׁוֹנִֽי
הֲנִסָּ֬ה דָבָ֣ר אֵלֶ֣יךָ תִּלְאֶ֑ה וַעְצֹ֥ר בְּ֝מִלִּ֗ין מִ֣י יוּכָֽל
כּ֭וֹשֵׁל יְקִימ֣וּן מִלֶּ֑יךָ וּבִרְכַּ֖יִם כֹּרְע֣וֹת תְּאַמֵּֽץ
הַלְהוֹכַ֣ח מִלִּ֣ים תַּחְשֹׁ֑בוּ וּ֝לְר֗וּחַ אִמְרֵ֥י נֹאָֽשׁ
הֲלֹא הֵ֣ם י֭וֹרוּךָ יֹ֣אמְרוּ לָ֑ךְ וּ֝מִלִּבָּ֗ם יוֹצִ֥אוּ מִלִּֽים
הֲלֹא אֹ֭זֶן מִלִּ֣ין תִּבְחָ֑ן וְ֝חֵ֗ךְ אֹ֣כֶל יִטְעַם לֽוֹ
שִׁמְע֣וּ שָׁ֭מוֹעַ מִלָּתִ֑י וְ֝אַֽחֲוָתִ֗י בְּאָזְנֵיכֶֽם
הוֹכֵ֣חַ בְּ֭דָבָר לֹ֣א יִסְכּ֑וֹן וּ֝מִלִּ֗ים לֹא יוֹעִ֥יל בָּֽם
כִּֽי תָשִׁ֣יב אֶל אֵ֣ל רוּחֶ֑ךָ וְהֹצֵ֖אתָ מִפִּ֣יךָ מִלִּֽין

וְזֶ֕ה אֲשֶׁ֥ר תַּֽעֲשֶׂ֖ה אֹתָ֑הּ שְׁלֹ֧שׁ מֵא֣וֹת אַמָּ֗ה אֹ֚רֶךְ הַתֵּבָ֔ה חֲמִשִּׁ֤ים אַמָּה֙ רָחְבָּ֔הּ וּשְׁלֹשִׁ֥ים אַמָּ֖ה קוֹמָתָֽהּ
צֹ֣הַר תַּֽעֲשֶׂ֣ה לַתֵּבָ֗ה וְאֶל אַמָּה֙ תְּכַלֶ֣נָּה מִלְמַ֔עְלָה וּפֶ֥תַח הַתֵּבָ֖ה בְּצִדָּ֣הּ תָּשִׂ֑ים תַּחְתִּיִּ֛ם שְׁנִיִּ֥ם וּשְׁלִשִׁ֖ים תַּֽעֲשֶֽׂהָ

וַיֹּ֤אמֶר יְהוָה֙ לְנֹ֔חַ בֹּֽא אַתָּ֥ה וְכָל בֵּיתְךָ֖ אֶל הַתֵּבָ֑ה כִּֽי אֹתְךָ֥ רָאִ֛יתִי צַדִּ֥יק לְפָנַ֖י בַּדּ֥וֹר הַזֶּֽה

וַֽיְהִ֧י הַמַּבּ֛וּל אַרְבָּעִ֥ים י֖וֹם עַל הָאָ֑רֶץ וַיִּרְבּ֣וּ הַמַּ֗יִם וַיִּשְׂאוּ֙ אֶת הַתֵּבָ֔ה וַתָּ֖רָם מֵעַ֥ל הָאָֽרֶץ

וַיִּ֜מַח אֶֽת כָּל הַיְק֣וּם אֲשֶׁ֣ר עַל פְּנֵ֣י הָֽאֲדָמָ֗ה מֵאָדָ֤ם עַד בְּהֵמָה֙ עַד רֶ֨מֶשׂ֙ וְעַד ע֣וֹף הַשָּׁמַ֔יִם וַיִּמָּח֖וּ מִן הָאָ֑רֶץ וַיִשָּׁ֧אֶר אַךְ נֹ֛חַ וַֽאֲשֶׁ֥ר אִתּ֖וֹ בַּתֵּבָֽה

וַיַּ֥רְא שַׂר הָאֹפִ֖ים כִּ֣י ט֣וֹב פָּתָ֑ר וַיֹּ֨אמֶר֙ אֶל יוֹסֵ֔ף אַף אֲנִי֙ בַּחֲלוֹמִ֔י וְהִנֵּ֗ה שְׁלֹשָׁ֛ה סַלֵּ֥י חֹרִ֖י עַל רֹאשִֽׁי
וְאֵ֛ת שַׂ֥ר הָאֹפִ֖ים תָּלָ֑ה כַּאֲשֶׁ֥ר פָּתַ֛ר לָהֶ֖ם יוֹסֵֽף
וַיְהִ֤י בַבֹּ֨קֶר֙ וַתִּפָּ֣עֶם רוּח֔וֹ וַיִּשְׁלַ֗ח וַיִּקְרָ֛א אֶת כָּל חַרְטֻמֵּ֥י מִצְרַ֖יִם וְאֶת כָּל חֲכָמֶ֑יהָ וַיְסַפֵּ֨ר פַּרְעֹ֤ה לָהֶם֙ אֶת חֲלֹמ֔וֹ וְאֵין פּוֹתֵ֥ר אוֹתָ֖ם לְפַרְעֹֽה
וְשָׁ֨ם אִתָּ֜נוּ נַ֣עַר עִבְרִ֗י עֶ֚בֶד לְשַׂ֣ר הַטַּבָּחִ֔ים וַנְּ֨סַפֶּר ל֔וֹ וַיִּפְתָּר לָ֖נוּ אֶת חֲלֹמֹתֵ֑ינוּ אִ֥ישׁ כַּחֲלֹמ֖וֹ פָּתָֽר
וַיְהִ֛י כַּאֲשֶׁ֥ר פָּֽתַר לָ֖נוּ כֵּ֣ן הָיָ֑ה אֹתִ֛י הֵשִׁ֥יב עַל כַּנִּ֖י וְאֹת֥וֹ תָלָֽה
וַיֹּ֤אמֶר פַּרְעֹה֙ אֶל יוֹסֵ֔ף חֲל֣וֹם חָלַ֔מְתִּי וּפֹתֵ֖ר אֵ֣ין אֹת֑וֹ וַאֲנִ֗י שָׁמַ֤עְתִּי עָלֶ֨יךָ֙ לֵאמֹ֔ר תִּשְׁמַ֥ע חֲל֖וֹם לִפְתֹּ֥ר אֹתֽוֹ

passages.text: אֶת הַמְּנֹרָ֨ה הַטְּהֹרָ֜ה אֶת נֵרֹתֶ֗יהָ נֵרֹ֛ת הַמַּֽעֲרָכָ֖ה וְאֶת כָּל כֵּלֶ֑יהָ וְאֵ֖ת שֶׁ֥מֶן הַמָּאֽוֹר
וְשַׂמְתָּ֥ אוֹתָ֛ם שְׁתַּ֥יִם מַֽעֲרָכ֖וֹת שֵׁ֣שׁ הַֽמַּעֲרָ֑כֶת עַ֛ל הַשֻּׁלְחָ֥ן הַטָּהֹ֖ר לִפְנֵ֥י יְהוָֽה
וּבָנִ֨יתָ מִזְבֵּ֜חַ לַיהוָ֣ה אֱלֹהֶ֗יךָ עַ֣ל רֹ֧אשׁ הַמָּע֛וֹז הַזֶּ֖ה בַּמַּֽעֲרָכָ֑ה וְלָֽקַחְתָּ֙ אֶת הַפָּ֣ר הַשֵּׁנִ֔י וְהַעֲלִ֣יתָ עוֹלָ֔ה בַּעֲצֵ֥י הָאֲשֵׁרָ֖ה אֲשֶׁ֥ר תִּכְרֹֽת
וַיַּעַרְכ֨וּ פְלִשְׁתִּ֜ים לִקְרַ֣את יִשְׂרָאֵ֗ל וַתִּטֹּשׁ֙ הַמִּלְחָמָ֔ה וַיִּנָּ֥גֶף יִשְׂרָאֵ֖ל לִפְנֵ֣י פְלִשְׁתִּ֑ים וַיַּכּ֤וּ בַמַּֽעֲרָכָה֙ בַּשָּׂדֶ֔ה כְּאַרְבַּ֥עַת אֲלָפִ֖ים אִֽישׁ
וַיָּ֤רָץ אִישׁ בִּנְיָמִן֙ מֵהַמַּ֣עֲרָכָ֔ה וַיָּבֹ֥א שִׁלֹ֖ה בַּיּ֣וֹם הַה֑וּא וּמַדָּ֣יו קְרֻעִ֔ים וַאֲדָמָ֖ה עַל רֹאשֽׁוֹ
וַיֹּ֨אמֶר הָאִ֜ישׁ אֶל עֵלִ֗י אָֽנֹכִי֙ הַבָּ֣א מִן הַמַּעֲרָכָ֔ה וַאֲנִ֕י מִן הַמַּעֲרָכָ֖ה נַ֣סְתִּי הַיּ֑וֹם וַיֹּ֛אמֶר מֶֽה הָיָ֥ה הַדָּבָ֖ר בְּנִֽי

וַֽיַּעֲמֹ֗ד וַיִּקְרָא֙ אֶל מַעַרְכֹ֣ת יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל וַיֹּ֣אמֶר לָהֶ֔ם לָ֥מָּה תֵצְא֖וּ לַעֲרֹ֣ךְ מִלְחָמָ֑ה הֲל֧וֹא אָנֹכִ֣י הַפְּלִשְׁתִּ֗י וְאַתֶּם֙ עֲבָדִ֣ים לְשָׁא֔וּל בְּרוּ לָכֶ֥ם אִ֖ישׁ וְיֵרֵ֥ד אֵלָֽי
וַיֹּ֨אמֶר֙ הַפְּלִשְׁתִּ֔י אֲנִ֗י חֵרַ֛פְתִּי אֶת מַעַרְכ֥וֹת יִשְׂרָאֵ֖ל הַיּ֣וֹם הַזֶּ֑ה תְּנוּ לִ֣י אִ֔ישׁ וְנִֽלָּחֲמָ֖ה יָֽחַד

וַיַּשְׁכֵּ֨ם דָּוִ֜ד בַּבֹּ֗קֶר וַיִּטֹּ֤שׁ אֶת הַצֹּאן֙ עַל שֹׁמֵ֔ר וַיִּשָּׂ֣א וַיֵּ֔לֶךְ כַּאֲשֶׁ֥ר צִוָּ֖הוּ יִשָׁ֑י וַיָּבֹא֙ הַמַּעְגָּ֔לָה וְהַחַ֗יִל הַיֹּצֵא֙ אֶל הַמַּ֣עֲרָכָ֔ה וְהֵרֵ֖עוּ בַּמִּלְחָמָֽה
וַתַּעֲרֹ֤ךְ יִשְׂרָאֵל֙ וּפְלִשְׁתִּ֔ים מַעֲרָכָ֖ה לִקְרַ֥את מַעֲרָכָֽה
וַיִּטֹּשׁ֩ דָּוִ֨ד אֶת הַכֵּלִ֜ים מֵעָלָ֗יו עַל יַד֙ שׁוֹמֵ֣ר הַכֵּלִ֔ים וַיָּ֖רָץ הַמַּעֲרָכָ֑ה וַיָּבֹ֕א וַיִּשְׁאַ֥ל לְאֶחָ֖יו לְשָׁלֽוֹם
וְה֣וּא מְדַבֵּ֣ר עִמָּ֗ם וְהִנֵּ֣ה אִ֣ישׁ הַבֵּנַ֡יִם עוֹלֶ֞ה גָּלְיָת֩ הַפְּלִשְׁתִּ֨י שְׁמ֤וֹ מִגַּת֙ ממערות מִמַּעַרְכ֣וֹת פְּלִשְׁתִּ֔ים וַיְדַבֵּ֖ר כַּדְּבָרִ֣ים הָאֵ֑לֶּה וַיִּשְׁמַ֖ע דָּוִֽד

וַיֹּ֣אמֶר דָּוִ֗ד אֶֽל הָאֲנָשִׁ֞ים הָעֹמְדִ֣ים עִמּוֹ֮ לֵאמֹר֒ מַה יֵּעָשֶׂ֗ה לָאִישׁ֙ אֲשֶׁ֤ר יַכֶּה֙ אֶת הַפְּלִשְׁתִּ֣י הַלָּ֔ז וְהֵסִ֥יר חֶרְפָּ֖ה מֵעַ֣ל יִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל כִּ֣י מִ֗י הַפְּלִשְׁתִּ֤י הֶֽעָרֵל֙ הַזֶּ֔ה כִּ֣י חֵרֵ֔ף מַעַרְכ֖וֹת אֱלֹהִ֥ים חַיִּֽים
גַּ֧ם אֶֽת הָאֲרִ֛י גַּם הַדּ֖וֹב הִכָּ֣ה עַבְדֶּ֑ךָ וְֽ֠הָיָה הַפְּלִשְׁתִּ֨י הֶעָרֵ֤ל הַזֶּה֙ כְּאַחַ֣ד מֵהֶ֔ם כִּ֣י חֵרֵ֔ף מַעַרְכֹ֖ת אֱלֹהִ֥ים חַיִּֽים
וַיֹּ֤אמֶר דָּוִד֙ אֶל הַפְּלִשְׁתִּ֔י אַתָּה֙ בָּ֣א אֵלַ֔י בְּחֶ֖רֶב וּבַחֲנִ֣ית וּבְכִיד֑וֹן וְאָנֹכִ֣י בָֽא אֵלֶ֗יךָ בְּשֵׁם֙ יְהוָ֣ה צְבָא֔וֹת אֱלֹהֵ֛י מַעַרְכ֥וֹת יִשְׂרָאֵ֖ל אֲשֶׁ֥ר חֵרַֽפְתָּ

leads.title: Satan refuses to bow to Adam
leads.summary: God commands the angels to honor Adam, and Satan refuses. Found in the Life of Adam and Eve and the Cave of Treasures, and repeatedly in the Quran.

passages.ref: Life of Adam and Eve (Latin Vita 12–16)

leads.title: The Kalam cosmological argument
leads.summary: The argument that the universe began and so has a cause, developed by the mutakallimūn and al-Ghazali, was revived and named by William Lane Craig in analytic philosophy of religion.

passages.ref: W. L. Craig, The Kalām Cosmological Argument (1979)

leads.title: Panchatantra to Kalila wa-Dimna
leads.summary: The Sanskrit Panchatantra was translated into Middle Persian (Burzoy, 6th c.), then Arabic (Ibn al-Muqaffaʿ, 8th c.), then into Hebrew, Greek, Latin, and most European languages.

leads.title: Kumarbi cycle and Hesiod's Theogony
leads.summary: Both have the same succession myth: Anu, Kumarbi, Teshub in the Hurro-Hittite cycle and Ouranos, Kronos, Zeus in Hesiod, including a sky god castrated by his successor.

leads.title: kursī: Sumerian throne to Quranic seat
leads.summary: Sumerian guza passed into Akkadian kussû, Aramaic kursēʾ, and Arabic kursī. The Quran's Throne Verse (2:255) uses it.

passages.note: His kursī encompasses the heavens and the earth
passages.text: ٱللَّهُ لَآ إِلَٰهَ إِلَّا هُوَ ٱلْحَىُّ ٱلْقَيُّومُ لَا تَأْخُذُهُۥ سِنَةٌ وَلَا نَوْمٌ لَّهُۥ مَا فِى ٱلسَّمَٰوَٰتِ وَمَا فِى ٱلْأَرْضِ مَن ذَا ٱلَّذِى يَشْفَعُ عِندَهُۥٓ إِلَّا بِإِذْنِهِۦ يَعْلَمُ مَا بَيْنَ أَيْدِيهِمْ وَمَا خَلْفَهُمْ وَلَا يُحِيطُونَ بِشَىْءٍ مِّنْ عِلْمِهِۦٓ إِلَّا بِمَا شَآءَ وَسِعَ كُرْسِيُّهُ ٱلسَّمَٰوَٰتِ وَٱلْأَرْضَ وَلَا يَـُٔودُهُۥ حِفْظُهُمَا وَهُوَ ٱلْعَلِىُّ ٱلْعَظِيمُ

passages.note: Solomon's kursī

evidence.text: Arabic kursī shows the Aramaic -r- form (dissimilated -ss- > -rs-), which points to Aramaic as the immediate source.

leads.title: Mani and the 'seal of the prophets'
leads.summary: Quran 33:40 calls Muhammad khātam al-nabiyyīn. Manichaean sources present Mani as the last in a line of prophets (Buddha, Zoroaster, Jesus), and whether 'seal' was a Manichaean title is debated.

passages.text: مَّا كَانَ مُحَمَّدٌ أَبَآ أَحَدٍ مِّن رِّجَالِكُمْ وَلَٰكِن رَّسُولَ ٱللَّهِ وَخَاتَمَ ٱلنَّبِيِّۦنَ وَكَانَ ٱللَّهُ بِكُلِّ شَىْءٍ عَلِيمًا

passages.ref: Kephalaia 1; al-Biruni's quotation of the Shābuhragān

evidence.text: See Stroumsa, 'Seal of the Prophets: The Nature of a Manichaean Metaphor' (1986), for the case against reading it as a Manichaean title.

leads.title: Mary raised in the Temple
leads.summary: The Protevangelium of James has Mary dedicated to the Temple, fed by an angel, and her guardian chosen by a sign. The Quran has Mary's dedication, miraculous provision in the sanctuary, Zechariah as guardian, and lots cast for her care.

passages.text: (3:35) إِذْ قَالَتِ ٱمْرَأَتُ عِمْرَٰنَ رَبِّ إِنِّى نَذَرْتُ لَكَ مَا فِى بَطْنِى مُحَرَّرًا فَتَقَبَّلْ مِنِّىٓ إِنَّكَ أَنتَ ٱلسَّمِيعُ ٱلْعَلِيمُ (3:36) فَلَمَّا وَضَعَتْهَا قَالَتْ رَبِّ إِنِّى وَضَعْتُهَآ أُنثَىٰ وَٱللَّهُ أَعْلَمُ بِمَا وَضَعَتْ وَلَيْسَ ٱلذَّكَرُ كَٱلْأُنثَىٰ وَإِنِّى سَمَّيْتُهَا مَرْيَمَ وَإِنِّىٓ أُعِيذُهَا بِكَ وَذُرِّيَّتَهَا مِنَ ٱلشَّيْطَٰنِ ٱلرَّجِيمِ (3:37) فَتَقَبَّلَهَا رَبُّهَا بِقَبُولٍ حَسَنٍ وَأَنۢبَتَهَا نَبَاتًا حَسَنًا وَكَفَّلَهَا زَكَرِيَّا كُلَّمَا دَخَلَ عَلَيْهَا زَكَرِيَّا ٱلْمِحْرَابَ وَجَدَ عِندَهَا رِزْقًا قَالَ يَٰمَرْيَمُ أَنَّىٰ لَكِ هَٰذَا قَالَتْ هُوَ مِنْ عِندِ ٱللَّهِ إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ يَرْزُقُ مَن يَشَآءُ بِغَيْرِ حِسَابٍ (3:44) ذَٰلِكَ مِنْ أَنۢبَآءِ ٱلْغَيْبِ نُوحِيهِ إِلَيْكَ وَمَا كُنتَ لَدَيْهِمْ إِذْ يُلْقُونَ أَقْلَٰمَهُمْ أَيُّهُمْ يَكْفُلُ مَرْيَمَ وَمَا كُنتَ لَدَيْهِمْ إِذْ يَخْتَصِمُونَ

leads.title: Mary and the palm tree
leads.summary: In Pseudo-Matthew a palm bends to feed Mary and a spring opens during the flight to Egypt. In the Quran a palm and a stream sustain Mary during the birth of Jesus.

Only in David's thanksgiving psalm (composite of Pss 105, 96, 106): A psalm sung in the narrative is stitched from passages found in the Psalter; Prayer: 'save us, gather us and deliver us from the nations'; Heavens, earth, sea, fields and trees rejoice and sing before the coming God; The patriarchs few in number wander from nation to nation, protected by God; All the people say 'Amen' and praise YHWH; 'Touch not my anointed ones, do my prophets no harm'; The world is firmly established and cannot be moved; Proclamation among the nations: 'YHWH is king' (YHWH malakh); God comes to judge the earth with righteousness, and all creation rejoices; Idols called 'elilim' ('nothings'); YHWH is great and to be feared above all gods; Refrain 'Give thanks to YHWH for he is good, for his steadfast love is forever'.

Only in Hypocrites and the call to judgment; 'we hear and obey'; the promise of succession: God promises the believers succession (istikhlāf) in the land as he gave it to those before them, exchanging fear for security; 'You are my witnesses,' says YHWH: before me no god was formed and after me there shall be none; Blessing: God removes harmful wild beasts from the land; This people honors God with lips while its heart is far; its fear of him is a commandment of men learned by rote; Believers' confession 'we hear and we obey' (sami'na wa-ata'na); The people answer as one: all that YHWH has spoken we will do.

evidence.text: Confirmed by a side-by-side reading of both originals (alignments/hb-quran/07-hb-quran.yaml): parallel. YHWH ʾên kāmôḵā wə-ʾên ʾĕlōhîm zûlāṯeḵā vs. huwa llāhu lladhī lā ilāha illā huwa (twice). David's prayer in the second person; the Quran's creed in the third.
Shared motifs, rarest first: 'There is none like you and no God beside you' (weight 5.8). Pair score 5.8.

Only in Nathan's oracle of an eternal house and David's prayer: Pun on 'house': the king would build God a house; God will build the king a house (dynasty); Revelation described as God 'uncovering the ear' of his servant; The king lives in a cedar house while the ark of God remains under curtains; God has never dwelt in a house but moved from tent to tent; God promises to make the chosen one's name great; Israel is the one nation on earth whom God went to redeem for himself; A prophet approves a plan, then is corrected by a revelation that night; God took the ruler from following the sheep; The king's son, not the king, will build the house for God's name; Prayer of humility: 'Who am I and what is my house?'; God declares the king his son: 'I will be his father and he my son'; God promises David's house and throne will endure forever; and 1 more.

Only in The hypocrites' false promises, Satan's disowning, the Quran on a mountain, and the litany of beautiful names: They fight only from fortified towns or behind walls; you think them united but their hearts are divided; Those who forgot God, so he made them forget themselves; Hypocrites promise their unbelieving allies to leave or fight with them, but will not; Let every soul look to what it has sent ahead for tomorrow; Had this Quran been sent down on a mountain you would see it humbled and split asunder for fear of God; Like Satan who says to man 'Disbelieve!' and when he disbelieves says 'I am quit of you, I fear God'; A mountain shaken by God's descent or by his revelation [divergence between the texts]; The mountain smokes like a furnace and quakes as God descends in fire; Litany of divine names: King, Holy, Peace, Faithful, Guardian, Mighty, Compeller, Proud, Creator, Maker, Fashioner; to him belong the most beautiful names; Do evildoers think God will make them equal to the righteous in life and in death?; Opening formula: whatever is in the heavens and the earth glorifies God (sabbaha / yusabbihu lillah).

passages.text: וַיָּ֨קָם דָּוִ֤יד הַמֶּ֨לֶךְ֙ עַל רַגְלָ֔יו וַיֹּ֕אמֶר שְׁמָע֖וּנִי אַחַ֣י וְעַמִּ֑י אֲנִ֣י עִם לְבָבִ֡י לִבְנוֹת֩ בֵּ֨ית מְנוּחָ֜ה לַאֲר֣וֹן בְּרִית יְהוָ֗ה וְלַהֲדֹם֙ רַגְלֵ֣י אֱלֹהֵ֔ינוּ וַהֲכִינ֖וֹתִי לִבְנֽוֹת

passages.note: The temple as a house of rest for the ark and the footstool of God's feet (kursi (Aramaic kursya, throne))
passages.text: ٱللَّهُ لَآ إِلَٰهَ إِلَّا هُوَ ٱلْحَىُّ ٱلْقَيُّومُ لَا تَأْخُذُهُۥ سِنَةٌ وَلَا نَوْمٌ لَّهُۥ مَا فِى ٱلسَّمَٰوَٰتِ وَمَا فِى ٱلْأَرْضِ مَن ذَا ٱلَّذِى يَشْفَعُ عِندَهُۥٓ إِلَّا بِإِذْنِهِۦ يَعْلَمُ مَا بَيْنَ أَيْدِيهِمْ وَمَا خَلْفَهُمْ وَلَا يُحِيطُونَ بِشَىْءٍ مِّنْ عِلْمِهِۦٓ إِلَّا بِمَا شَآءَ وَسِعَ كُرْسِيُّهُ ٱلسَّمَٰوَٰتِ وَٱلْأَرْضَ وَلَا يَـُٔودُهُۥ حِفْظُهُمَا وَهُوَ ٱلْعَلِىُّ ٱلْعَظِيمُ

evidence.text: Shared motifs, rarest first: The temple as a house of rest for the ark and the footstool of God's feet (weight 6.7). Pair score 6.7.

Only in David's assembly speech and the written pattern of the temple: The cherubim over the ark are called 'the chariot' (merkavah); God's election narrows from tribe to family to man to the chosen son; Eunuchs (sarisim) serve among the royal officials; Multiple gold and silver lampstands and tables in the temple; The Davidic king sits on 'the throne of YHWH'; The king may not build the temple because he is a man of war who shed much blood; Formula: be strong and courageous, do not fear, God will not leave or forsake you; The dynasty's continuance is conditioned on the heirs' faithfulness; God looks on the heart, not on appearance or height; God declares the king his son: 'I will be his father and he my son'; The sanctuary is built after a pattern shown by God on the mountain.

Only in Ranks of the messengers and the Throne Verse: God's footstool or seat (kursi) extends over the heavens and the earth; No compulsion in religion; Neither slumber nor sleep overtakes God; God's throne in relation to heaven and earth [divergence between the texts]; Whoever rejects false gods (taghut) and believes in God grasps the firmest handhold that never breaks; God does not slumber or sleep [divergence between the texts]; The guardian of Israel neither slumbers nor sleeps; A day comes with no trade, no friendship and no intercession; Jesus son of Mary given clear signs and supported with the holy spirit (ruh al-qudus); Israel's God is called 'the living God, enduring forever, whose kingdom shall never be destroyed'; God ranked some messengers above others; to some God spoke; God the Ever-Living, the Self-Subsisting (al-hayy al-qayyum); and 4 more.

passages.note: Donors confess that everything comes from God and they only give back what is his (wa-btaghi fīmā ātāka llāhu d-dāra l-ākhirata ... wa-aḥsin kamā aḥsana llāhu ilayka ~ wə-hā-ʿōšer wə-hak-kāvôd mil-ləfānêkā ... kî mimməkā hak-kōl û-mi-yyādəkā nātannû lākh: wealth is God's gift and should be used toward God; David's people give back from it, Qārūn is told to and refuses.)

evidence.text: Confirmed by a side-by-side reading of both originals (alignments/hb-quran/05-hb-quran.yaml): echo. wa-btaghi fīmā ātāka llāhu d-dāra l-ākhirata ... wa-aḥsin kamā aḥsana llāhu ilayka ~ wə-hā-ʿōšer wə-hak-kāvôd mil-ləfānêkā ... kî mimməkā hak-kōl û-mi-yyādəkā nātannû lākh: wealth is God's gift and should be used toward God; David's people give back from it, Qārūn is told to and refuses.
Shared motifs, rarest first: Donors confess that everything comes from God and they only give back what is his (weight 6.7). Pair score 6.7.

Only in Free-will gifts, David's doxology, Solomon enthroned again, David's death: Persian darics (adarkonim) are counted among offerings in David's time; God is addressed as 'our father' in prayer; The king is made king and anointed a second time; The king gives his own private treasure (segullah) for the temple; 'Our days on earth are like a shadow, and there is no hope'; Princes 'give the hand' under the new king in allegiance; The assembly bows down to YHWH and to the king; Onyx, inlay, antimony, multicolored stones and marble gathered for the temple; The temple is called the birah (fortress/palace), not for man but for God; A thousand bulls, a thousand rams and a thousand lambs offered in a day; Doxology: 'Yours, YHWH, is the greatness, the power, the glory, the victory and the majesty ... and the kingdom'; To God belongs the grandeur (kibriya') in the heavens and the earth; and 10 more.

Only in Qarun's treasures and his swallowing by the earth; closing: God who imposed the Quran will bring the prophet back to a place of return (maʿād); Qārūn says his wealth came to him through knowledge he possesses; Qārūn (Korah) of Moses' people was given treasures whose keys would weigh down a band of strong men; Bystanders of a divine punishment fear it could have struck them too; Qārūn goes out in his finery and the worldly wish for his fortune; What Korah's sin was, and why the earth swallowed him [divergence between the texts]; All on earth perish; there remains the Face of your Lord, possessor of majesty and honor; Warning against saying my power and the might of my hand made this wealth; The rich man's wealth is his strong city; the poverty of the poor is their ruin; The earth opens its mouth and swallows rebels alive into Sheol.

passages.note: A daughter of Pharaoh (Bithiah) marries an Israelite
passages.text: וְאִשְׁתּ֣וֹ הַיְהֻדִיָּ֗ה יָלְדָ֞ה אֶת יֶ֨רֶד אֲבִ֤י גְדוֹר֙ וְאֶת חֶ֨בֶר֙ אֲבִ֣י שׂוֹכ֔וֹ וְאֶת יְקֽוּתִיאֵ֖ל אֲבִ֣י זָנ֑וֹחַ וְאֵ֗לֶּה בְּנֵי֙ בִּתְיָ֣ה בַת פַּרְעֹ֔ה אֲשֶׁ֥ר לָקַ֖ח מָֽרֶד

Only in Clans of Judah; the prayer of Jabez; craft guilds; Bithiah daughter of Pharaoh: Gloss: 'and the records/words are ancient'; Clans as hereditary guilds (linen-workers, potters) who dwelt with the king in his work; Man named for his mother's pain (otsev) prays to be blessed, have his border enlarged and be kept from pain, and God grants it; A place called 'Valley of Craftsmen' because its founders were craftsmen; The hero's previously unnamed mother is named in a genealogy; Founder figure called 'father' of a town (father of Bethlehem, Tekoa, Kiriath-jearim); A lone daughter is named in a male genealogy (Dinah, Serah).

Only in Al-Tahrim: the prohibited thing and the divulged secret; fire fed with stones; the wives of Noah and Lot, Pharaoh's wife and Mary daughter of 'Imran: If he divorced them, God might give him in exchange better wives: submitting, believing, devout, repentant, worshipping, fasting/wandering (sa'ihat), previously married and virgins; A Fire whose fuel is people and stones, over which are harsh, stern angels who never disobey God; If two wives back each other against him, God is his protector, and Gabriel, the righteous believers and the angels; Mary, daughter of 'Imran, guarded her chastity; God breathed into it of his spirit, and she believed the words of her Lord and his books; Pharaoh's wife prays 'My Lord, build me a house with you in the Garden and save me from Pharaoh and his deeds'; The believers pray on the day: 'Our Lord, perfect our light for us and forgive us'; 'O Prophet, why do you forbid what God made lawful for you, seeking to please your wives?'; God has ordained the dissolution of oaths; Turn to God in sincere repentance (tawba nasuh); The prophet confided a secret to one of his wives; she divulged it, and God informed him; The wives of Noah and Lot, married to righteous servants, betrayed them and are told to enter the Fire; Father or husband may annul a woman's vow on the day he hears it; A man's vow or oath must be fulfilled as uttered [contrast between the texts]; and 10 more.

As in 2Chr 9:8: the Kings queen blesses 'YHWH your God' for loving Israel and setting Solomon on the throne of Israel; the Quran's queen submits with Solomon to the Lord of the worlds. A foreigner's praise of Israel's God becomes a conversion to the universal Lord.

Shared motifs, rarest first: A foreign queen tests the king with riddles and he answers them all (weight 6.3); What the queen of Sheba says of Solomon's God [divergence between the texts] (weight 6.3). Pair score 12.6.

Only in The Queen of Sheba visits Solomon: Visitor confesses that reports did not tell even half of the king's wisdom and wealth; Rare almug wood from Ophir used for temple supports and lyres for singers; never seen again; A visitor seeing the king's court is left breathless ('no more spirit in her'); A royal visitor arrives with camels carrying spices, gold and precious stones; A foreigner declares that YHWH is greater than all gods; Fleets with Phoenician sailors sail from the Red Sea to Ophir and bring back gold; Kings of all the earth send to hear the wise king's wisdom.

Only in Solomon, the speech of birds, the ants, the hoopoe and the Queen of Sheba: Entering Solomon's palace, the queen takes its floor of smooth glass for a pool and bares her legs; The hoopoe returns with sure news from Sabaʾ, knowledge Solomon lacked; Solomon sends the hoopoe to drop his letter before the queen and wait for their reply; Solomon reviews the birds, finds the hoopoe absent and threatens to punish or slaughter it unless it brings a clear excuse; An ʿifrīt of the jinn offers to bring the queen's throne before Solomon rises from his seat; Solomon's letter begins 'In the name of God, the Merciful, the Compassionate' and demands submission; The queen sends a gift to see what the envoys bring back; Solomon rejects the wealth and threatens invasion; The queen confesses she wronged herself and submits with Solomon to God, Lord of the worlds; Solomon has the queen's throne disguised to test whether she recognizes it; she says 'It is as though it were it'; The queen and her people prostrate to the sun instead of God; Solomon inherits from David (knowledge and kingship); Solomon prays to be inspired to thank God for favor to him and his parents and to be admitted among the righteous; and 21 more.

evidence.text: Shared motifs, rarest first: King keeps tens of thousands of chariot horses and horsemen (weight 6.3); King must not multiply horses, wives or silver and gold, nor return the people to Egypt (weight 5.3). Pair score 11.6.

Only in Solomon's gold, ivory throne, fleet and horse trade: Gold coming to the king each year weighs 666 talents; King makes hundreds of shields of beaten gold and hangs them in the palace; King's merchants import horses from Egypt and Kue and export chariots to Hittite and Aramean kings at fixed prices; Great ivory throne overlaid with gold, with six steps and twelve lions on the steps and two beside the arms; Tarshish ships every three years bring gold, silver, ivory, apes and peacocks (or baboons); The king makes silver and gold as common as stones and cedar as sycamores; Kings of all the earth send to hear the wise king's wisdom.

Only in Solomon's steeds, the body on his throne, and the unmatched kingdom: God tested Solomon by placing a body (jasad) on his throne; then he repented; Devils serve Solomon as builders and divers, and others are bound together in fetters; Solomon asks for a kingdom such as no one after him should have; Fine steeds shown to Solomon in the evening distract him from remembrance of God until the sun hides; he has them brought back and strokes (or slashes) their legs and necks; Solomon's horses [divergence between the texts]; What Solomon asks of God and the gift none after him will match [divergence between the texts]; The stormy wind is subjected to Solomon, blowing at his command; The enemy's horses are hamstrung and their chariots burned by divine command; Devils (shayāṭīn) and jinn labor for Solomon, diving and building.

Miṣrayim ʾel Parʿōh: a hunted young man flees by way of Midian. Hadad's route goes the opposite way, from Edom through Midian into Pharaoh's court, while Moses flees from Pharaoh's court to Midian.

passages.note: How Solomon died and how his death became known [divergence between the texts] (Solomon's death. 1 Kgs: wa-yyiškaḇ šəlōmōh ʿim-ʾăḇōṯâw wa-yyiqqāḇēr bə-ʿîr dāwiḏ, a plain death, burial and succession (after his apostasy and the tearing of the kingdom, 11:11). Only in Ahijah tears the cloak; Jeroboam flees; Solomon's death: The man designated to be king flees to Egypt (to Shishak) from the reigning king's attempt to kill him; Prophet tears a new garment into twelve pieces and gives ten to the future king as sign of the divided kingdom; God promises a lasting dynasty ('sure house') on condition of obedience; The king reigns forty years; A key figure is identified as the son of a widow; A torn robe-hem signifies the kingdom torn away; One tribe is left to the dynasty so that David may always have a 'lamp' (nir) in Jerusalem; Narrator refers the reader to a lost source book (Book of the Acts of Solomon, Chronicles of the Kings).

passages.note: Whether Solomon turned from God [response between the texts] (1Kgs 11:4-6 nāšāyw hiṭṭû ʾet lĕbābô ʾaḥărê ʾĕlōhîm ʾăḥērîm ... wa-yyaʿaś šĕlōmōh hā-raʿ bĕ-ʿênê YHWH: Solomon himself turns to other gods and God is angry with him (11:9); Q 2:102 wa-mā kafara sulaymānu wa-lākinna sh-shayāṭīna kafarū: 'Solomon did not disbelieve, it was the devils who disbelieved'. evidence.text: Confirmed by a side-by-side reading of both originals (alignments/hb-quran/04-hb-quran.yaml): echo. A public contest set before the assembled people between God's prophet and the king's religious professionals, ending with the people falling down and confessing: wayyippəlû ʿal-pənêhem wayyōʾmərû YHWH hûʾ hāʾĕlōhîm; fa-ulqiya s-saḥaratu sujjadan qālū āmannā bi-rabbi Hārūna wa-Mūsā. At Carmel the losers are killed by Elijah; in Q the converts are threatened by Pharaoh.
Shared motifs, rarest first: Prophet's wonders are imitated by the king's magicians in a contest (weight 5.1). Pair score 5.1.

Only in Contest on Mount Carmel: Prophet repairs the ruined altar with twelve stones for the tribes of Jacob; Contest of gods: the god who answers by fire on an unlit sacrifice is God; The prophets of Baal are seized and slaughtered at the brook Kishon; Prophets of Baal limp-dance around the altar and gash themselves with swords and lances till blood flows; Prophet mocks the silent god: perhaps he is musing, relieving himself, travelling, or asleep and must be woken; Sacrifice and altar drenched with four jars of water three times, filling a trench, before the miracle; The people fall on their faces crying 'YHWH, he is God! YHWH, he is God!'; How a public contest between God's prophet and the king's religious specialists ends [contrast between the texts]; An offering consumed by fire as proof of the true God or messenger [response between the texts]; Fire from heaven falls and consumes the offering, wood, stones, dust and water; 'How long will you hop between two branches? If YHWH is God, follow him; if Baal, follow him'; A single prophet of YHWH stands against 450 prophets of Baal and 400 of Asherah; and 10 more.

Only in Moses and Aaron before Pharaoh; the contest with the magicians: The contest with the magicians is set for a festival day (yawm al-zīna) at forenoon with the people assembled; From the earth humans were created, into it they return, and from it they are brought forth again; Formula: 'Peace be on whoever follows the guidance'; Pharaoh asks about the fate of former generations; the answer: their knowledge is with God in a book; The prophets are told to speak to the tyrant with gentle words, that he may take heed or fear; The defeated magicians fall prostrate and declare faith in the Lord of Moses and Aaron [divergence between the texts]; The magicians' ropes and staffs appear by sorcery to be moving like snakes; Condemned believers tell the tyrant 'decree what you will; you can only decree for this worldly life'; Pharaoh threatens the converted magicians with cutting off hands and feet on opposite sides and crucifixion (on palm trunks); King defies the prophet: 'Who is YHWH that I should obey him?' [divergence between the texts]; God made the earth a cradle (mahd) or bed and laid out paths in it; Prophet delivers God's demand 'Let my people go that they may serve me' [divergence between the texts]; and 10 more.

Ahab says 'troubler' (ʿōkhēr), Thamūd use bird-augury language (iṭṭayyara, 'to take an ill omen'); Elijah blames their apostasy, Ṣāliḥ says their omen is with God.
Shared motifs, rarest first: King calls the prophet 'troubler of Israel' (okher Yisra'el); prophet returns the charge (weight 6.7). Pair score 6.7.

Only in Contest on Mount Carmel: Prophet repairs the ruined altar with twelve stones for the tribes of Jacob; Contest of gods: the god who answers by fire on an unlit sacrifice is God; The prophets of Baal are seized and slaughtered at the brook Kishon; Prophets of Baal limp-dance around the altar and gash themselves with swords and lances till blood flows; Prophet mocks the silent god: perhaps he is musing, relieving himself, travelling, or asleep and must be woken; Sacrifice and altar drenched with four jars of water three times, filling a trench, before the miracle; The people fall on their faces crying 'YHWH, he is God! YHWH, he is God!'; How a public contest between God's prophet and the king's religious specialists ends [contrast between the texts]; An offering consumed by fire as proof of the true God or messenger [response between the texts]; Fire from heaven falls and consumes the offering, wood, stones, dust and water; 'How long will you hop between two branches? If YHWH is God, follow him; if Baal, follow him'; A single prophet of YHWH stands against 450 prophets of Baal and 400 of Asherah; and 10 more.

Only in Salih, the evil omen and the nine plotters of Thamud: The people say they augur ill (iṭṭayyarnā) of the prophet; he answers that their omen (ṭāʾir) is with God; The men of the prophet's hometown seek his life: 'Do not prophesy in YHWH's name or you will die by our hand'; Nine men of the city swear by God to attack the prophet and his family by night and deny it to his avenger; The prophet Ṣāliḥ is sent to the people of Thamūd; They plot a plot, and God plots a plot; give the deniers respite a little; Formula: 'their brother' (akhūhum) Noah/Hud/Salih/Lot is a trustworthy messenger sent to his people; The listeners walk among the dwellings of generations God destroyed, a sign.

leads.title: Contest on Mount Carmel ↔ Misers, those who called God poor, and the fire-consumed offering
leads.summary: These two units share 2 motifs: an offering consumed by fire as proof of the true god or messenger [response between the texts], fire from heaven falls and consumes the offering, wood, stones, dust and water.

passages.note: An offering consumed by fire as proof of the true God or messenger [response between the texts] (1Kgs 18:24, 38 wĕ-hāyâ hā-ʾĕlōhîm ʾăšer yaʿăneh bā-ʾēš hûʾ hā-ʾĕlōhîm ... wa-ttippōl ʾēš YHWH wa-ttōʾkal ʾet hā-ʿōlâ: the god who answers by fire is God, and the fire eats the offering; Q 3:183 qālū inna llāha ʿahida ilaynā allā nuʾmina li-rasūlin ḥattā yaʾtiyanā bi-qurbānin taʾkuluhu n-nāru qul qad jāʾakum rusulun min qablī bi-l-bayyināti wa-bi-lladhī qultum fa-li-ma qataltumūhum: they claim God made them promise to believe no messenger without an offering 'the fire eats' (ʾākal / akala); answer: messengers did bring it, so why did you kill them? leads.title: Contest on Mount Carmel ↔ The people of the town, the three messengers and the man who came running
leads.summary: These two units share 1 motifs: the townsfolk say 'we augur ill of you' and threaten to stone the messengers; they reply 'your omen is with you'.

passages.text: وَلَا تَتَمَنَّوْا۟ مَا فَضَّلَ ٱللَّهُ بِهِۦ بَعْضَكُمْ عَلَىٰ بَعْضٍ لِّلرِّجَالِ نَصِيبٌ مِّمَّا ٱكْتَسَبُوا۟ وَلِلنِّسَآءِ نَصِيبٌ مِّمَّا ٱكْتَسَبْنَ وَسْـَٔلُوا۟ ٱللَّهَ مِن فَضْلِهِۦٓ إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ كَانَ بِكُلِّ شَىْءٍ عَلِيمًا

passages.note: Prohibitions of murder, adultery, theft and false witness
passages.text: וְ֠הוֹשִׁיבוּ שְׁנַ֨יִם אֲנָשִׁ֥ים בְּנֵֽי בְלִיַּעַל֮ נֶגְדּוֹ֒ וִיעִדֻ֣הוּ לֵאמֹ֔ר בֵּרַ֥כְתָּ אֱלֹהִ֖ים וָמֶ֑לֶךְ וְהוֹצִיאֻ֥הוּ וְסִקְלֻ֖הוּ וְיָמֹֽת

passages.note: Prohibitions of murder, adultery, theft and false witness
passages.text: וַ֠יָּבֹאוּ שְׁנֵ֨י הָאֲנָשִׁ֥ים בְּנֵֽי בְלִיַּעַל֮ וַיֵּשְׁב֣וּ נֶגְדּוֹ֒ וַיְעִדֻהוּ֩ אַנְשֵׁ֨י הַבְּלִיַּ֜עַל אֶת נָב֗וֹת נֶ֤גֶד הָעָם֙ לֵאמֹ֔ר בֵּרַ֥ךְ נָב֛וֹת אֱלֹהִ֖ים וָמֶ֑לֶךְ וַיֹּצִאֻ֨הוּ֙ מִח֣וּץ לָעִ֔יר וַיִּסְקְלֻ֥הוּ בָאֲבָנִ֖ים וַיָּמֹֽת

passages.note: Prohibitions of murder, adultery, theft and false witness (Exod 20:13, 15 lōʾ tirṣāḥ ... lōʾ tignōb; Q 4:29 lā taʾkulū amwālakum baynakum bi-l-bāṭili illā an takūna tijāratan ʿan tarāḍin minkum wa-lā taqtulū anfusakum: no wrongful taking of wealth (except by consented trade) and no killing, side by side as in the Decalogue.)
passages.text: يَٰٓأَيُّهَا ٱلَّذِينَ ءَامَنُوا۟ لَا تَأْكُلُوٓا۟ أَمْوَٰلَكُم بَيْنَكُم بِٱلْبَٰطِلِ إِلَّآ أَن تَكُونَ تِجَٰرَةً عَن تَرَاضٍ مِّنكُمْ وَلَا تَقْتُلُوٓا۟ أَنفُسَكُمْ إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ كَانَ بِكُمْ رَحِيمًا

evidence.text: Shared motifs, rarest first: Prohibition of coveting the neighbor's wife and property (weight 5.8); Prohibitions of murder, adultery, theft and false witness (weight 5.1). Pair score 10.9.

Only in Naboth's vineyard: Commoner refuses to sell or trade his ancestral vineyard to the king: 'God forbid I give you my fathers' inheritance'; Thwarted king lies on his bed, turns his face to the wall and refuses to eat; Queen writes letters in the king's name, sealed with his seal, ordering a judicial murder; A fast is proclaimed and two worthless men falsely testify that the victim 'blessed (cursed) God and king'; Innocent victim is taken outside the city and stoned to death; King goes home 'sullen and angry' (sar ve-za'ef) after a prophet's rebuke; Offender stoned to death by the community.

Only in Wealth by consent, major sins, and discord in marriage: Command: do not kill yourselves (or one another); In marital discord an arbiter is sent from his family and one from hers; If the major sins (kabāʾir) are avoided, God expiates lesser misdeeds; Men are maintainers (qawwāmūn) of women by God's preference and their spending; A wife whose rebellion (nushūz) is feared is admonished, left alone in bed, then struck; Those bound to you by oath-alliance receive their share; Prohibition of coveting the neighbor's wife and property [divergence between the texts]; The ground of a husband's authority over his wife [divergence between the texts]; Do not consume one another's wealth wrongfully (bil-bāṭil), only by trade with mutual consent.
Naboth's vineyard: tagged by Claude (model), reading the Hebrew.
Wealth by consent, major sins, and discord in marriage: tagged by Claude (model), reading the Arabic.

leads.title: Micaiah son of Imlah and the lying spirit ↔ Micaiah ben Imlah, the lying spirit in the divine council, and Ahab's death
leads.summary: These two units share 7 motifs: a spirit volunteers in the divine council to be a lying spirit in the prophets' mouths, court prophet makes iron horns: 'with these you will gore aram', four hundred court prophets unanimously promise victory, a false prophet strikes the true prophet on the cheek….

passages.note: A spirit volunteers in the divine council to be a lying spirit in the prophets' mouths
passages.text: (22:22) וַיֹּ֗אמֶר אֵצֵא֙ וְהָיִ֨יתִי֙ ר֣וּחַ שֶׁ֔קֶר בְּפִ֖י כָּל נְבִיאָ֑יו וַיֹּ֗אמֶר תְּפַתֶּה֙ וְגַם תּוּכָ֔ל צֵ֖א וַעֲשֵׂה כֵֽן (22:23) וְעַתָּ֗ה הִנֵּ֨ה נָתַ֤ן יְהוָה֙ ר֣וּחַ שֶׁ֔קֶר בְּפִ֖י כָּל נְבִיאֶ֣יךָ אֵ֑לֶּה וַֽיהוָ֔ה דִּבֶּ֥ר עָלֶ֖יךָ רָעָֽה

evidence.text: Shared motifs, rarest first: A round vessel ten cubits across measures thirty around (pi taken as three) (weight 6.7); Bronze vessels cast in the clay ground of the Jordan plain between Succoth and Zarethan (weight 6.7); The bronze used for the sanctuary is so abundant its weight was not determined (weight 6.7); An accounting of the gold, silver and bronze used for the sanctuary (weight 6.3); A gold table with the bread of the presence always before God (weight 6.0); A great cast-bronze 'sea' basin rests on twelve bronze oxen facing the four directions in threes (weight 6.0). Pair score 38.4.

Only in The bronze sea, wheeled stands and temple vessels: Ten golden lampstands stand before the inner sanctuary, five on each side; Ten wheeled bronze stands decorated with lions, oxen, cherubim and palms carry basins; How Solomon's great bronze works were produced [divergence between the texts]; Exact dimensions in cubits are given for a sacred object of the sanctuary; A bronze laver where priests wash hands and feet before service, lest they die; A small gold-plated altar for burning incense before the veil.

Only in Bronze altar, the molten sea on twelve oxen, lavers, lampstands and tables: A great bronze altar twenty cubits square and ten high; The temple has a court of the priests and a great court; The rim of the bronze sea is shaped like a lily blossom; The bronze sea serves for the priests to wash in, the lavers for rinsing offerings; Ten gold lampstands and ten tables, five on each side; Two named bronze pillars, Jachin and Boaz, before the temple.

leads.title: The bronze sea, wheeled stands and temple vessels ↔ David's mountains and mail; Solomon's wind, copper, jinn and staff
leads.summary: These two units share 2 motifs: how solomon's great bronze works were produced [divergence between the texts], a great cast-bronze 'sea' basin rests on twelve bronze oxen facing the four directions in threes.

passages.note: How Solomon's great bronze works were produced [divergence between the texts] (Solomon's cast bronze. 1 Kgs: wa-yyaʿaś ʾeṯ-ha-yyām mûṣāq ... ʿōmēḏ ʿal-šənê ʿāśār bāqār; bə-kikkar ha-yyardēn yəṣāqām ha-mmeleḵ bə-maʿăḇēh hā-ʾăḏāmâ (cast in clay moulds in the Jordan plain). Q: wa-asalnā lahu ʿayna l-qiṭr (God makes a spring of molten copper flow for him) ... wa-jifānin ka-l-jawābi wa-qudūrin rāsiyāt. The metal comes from a miraculous spring instead of the foundry, and the 'sea' and its stands are matched by basins like reservoirs and fixed cauldrons. Lead: identification of the jifān/qudūr with the yām and mekonot is a proposal.)

Solomon's cast bronze. 1 Kgs: wa-yyaʿaś ʾeṯ-ha-yyām mûṣāq ... ʿōmēḏ ʿal-šənê ʿāśār bāqār; bə-kikkar ha-yyardēn yəṣāqām ha-mmeleḵ bə-maʿăḇēh hā-ʾăḏāmâ (cast in clay moulds in the Jordan plain). Q: wa-asalnā lahu ʿayna l-qiṭr (God makes a spring of molten copper flow for him) ... wa-jifānin ka-l-jawābi wa-qudūrin rāsiyāt. The metal comes from a miraculous spring instead of the foundry, and the 'sea' and its stands are matched by basins like reservoirs and fixed cauldrons. Lead: identification of the jifān/qudūr with the yām and mekonot is a proposal.

Only in The bronze sea, wheeled stands and temple vessels: Ten golden lampstands stand before the inner sanctuary, five on each side; Ten wheeled bronze stands decorated with lions, oxen, cherubim and palms carry basins; The bronze used for the sanctuary is so abundant its weight was not determined; Bronze vessels cast in the clay ground of the Jordan plain between Succoth and Zarethan; A round vessel ten cubits across measures thirty around (pi taken as three); Exact dimensions in cubits are given for a sacred object of the sanctuary; An accounting of the gold, silver and bronze used for the sanctuary; A bronze laver where priests wash hands and feet before service, lest they die; A small gold-plated altar for burning incense before the veil; A gold table with the bread of the presence always before God.

Only in David's mountains and mail; Solomon's wind, copper, jinn and staff: God made a spring of molten copper (or brass) flow for Solomon; The jinn did not know the unseen, else they would not have stayed in humiliating labor; Solomon dies leaning on his staff; only a creature of the earth gnawing the staff reveals his death when he falls; David and the coat of mail [contrast between the texts]; How Solomon died and how his death became known [divergence between the texts]; Rivers clap their hands and mountains sing together before YHWH; God taught David the craft of making coats of mail; Who did Solomon's building and craft work [divergence between the texts]; The stormy wind is subjected to Solomon, blowing at his command; Mountains and birds are made to glorify God together with David; Devils (shayāṭīn) and jinn labor for Solomon, diving and building; Two golden cherubim face each other with wings spread over the ark.

Only in The ark brought into the temple; the cloud fills the house: Ark brought in procession into the temple at the autumn feast in the seventh month; Ends of the ark's poles visible from the holy place but not outside, 'to this day'; Sheep and cattle sacrificed so many that they could not be counted; Temple called a 'house of zebul' (exalted dwelling), a place for God to dwell forever; God has said he will dwell in thick darkness ('arafel); Archaic (Canaanite/Phoenician) month names Ziv, Bul and Ethanim are used; The tablets of the testimony are placed inside the ark; The cloud and glory fill the sanctuary so that even the leader cannot enter; Two golden cherubim face each other with wings spread over the ark.

Only in Talut (Saul), the ark and Jalut (Goliath): The ark (tabut) returns, carried by angels, containing tranquility (sakina) and relics left by the family of Moses and Aaron; David kills Jalut (Goliath) and is given kingship and wisdom; Were it not for God checking people by means of others, the earth would be corrupted; 'How many a small band has overcome a large one by God's leave'; God chose the king and increased him in knowledge and stature, though he lacked wealth; The people object that the chosen king has no wealth and they have more right to kingship; Before battle the army is tested at a river: whoever drinks is not with the leader, except a handful scooped by hand; The ark of the covenant: a gold-plated acacia chest with rings and poles [divergence between the texts]; David kills the Philistine giant [divergence between the texts]; A giant taunts Israel and is killed by a hero; A jar of manna preserved before the testimony for future generations; Objection raised against the newly chosen king [divergence between the texts]; and 10 more.

evidence.text: Shared motifs, rarest first: A foreigner from a far land who hears of God's name comes to pray at the temple and is heard (weight 6.7); 'There is no man who does not sin' (weight 6.7); Heaven and the heaven of heavens cannot contain God, much less a temple (weight 6.3); The direction faced in prayer [divergence between the texts] (weight 6.0); Prayers made toward the temple (or toward the land, city and house when in exile) are heard in heaven (weight 6.0); Prophet spreads out his palms to God in prayer (weight 5.4); Heaven and the heaven of heavens belong to God (weight 5.4). Pair score 42.5.

Only in Solomon's prayer of dedication: Exiles in an enemy land turn back with all their heart and pray toward their land, and God grants them mercy before captors; A man accused swears a curse-oath before the altar, and God judges guilty and innocent; Long catalogue of curses for covenant violation (disease, defeat, famine, exile); Egypt called an iron furnace (smelting furnace); Heaven is shut and no rain falls because of the people's sin; repentance brings rain; God alone knows the hearts of all humans.

Only in Solomon's blessing and dedication prayer on the bronze platform: Prayer lists famine, pestilence, blight, mildew, locust, siege and sickness as occasions for prayer; The king kneels on a bronze platform in the court and spreads his hands to heaven; An oath sworn before God's altar in the temple, judged by God; People away from Jerusalem or in exile pray in the direction of the land, city and temple; Captives confess in exile 'We have sinned, done wrong and acted wickedly'; 'Arise, YHWH, to your resting place, you and the ark of your might'; Temple called a 'house of zebul' (exalted dwelling), a place for God to dwell forever; 'O my servants who have transgressed against themselves, do not despair of God's mercy; God forgives all sins'; God has said he will dwell in thick darkness ('arafel); The dynasty's continuance is conditioned on the heirs' faithfulness; God looks on the heart, not on appearance or height; Sacrifice only at the place God will choose to make his name dwell; and 1 more.

evidence.text: Confirmed by a side-by-side reading of both originals (alignments/hb-quran/03-hb-quran.yaml): contrast. Opposite rulings on the prophet's intercession for a sinful people: Samuel calls it a sin to stop (ḥālîlāh llî mēḥăṭōʾ laYHWH mēḥădōl lᵉhitpallēl bᵉʿadkem); Q tells the prophet his prayer for the hypocrites is in vain (istaghfir lahum aw lā tastaghfir lahum).
Shared motifs, rarest first: Whether the prophet should intercede for a sinful people [contrast between the texts] (weight 6.7). Pair score 6.7.

Only in Samuel's farewell speech and the sign of thunder: Departing leader challenges the people: whose ox or donkey have I taken, from whom a bribe?; Prophet declares it would be a sin to cease praying for the people; Prophet calls down thunder and rain out of season, at wheat harvest, as a sign; Leader protests he never took so much as a donkey from anyone; Asking for a human king is a rejection of God's kingship; People put away foreign gods (Baals and Ashtaroth) at a prophet's call; Recital of history as cycle of sin, oppression, outcry and deliverance.

Only in The broken vow of charity; seventy prayers in vain: Hypocrites mock believers who give voluntarily and those who can give only their effort; Men vow to give alms if God enriches them, then turn miserly, and God sets hypocrisy in their hearts; Better not to vow than to vow and not pay; Hero vows that if God protects and provides for him, he will worship and tithe [divergence between the texts]; Even if the prophet asks forgiveness for them seventy times God will not forgive them; God is near in their mouths but far from their kidneys (hearts); Pay vows without delay; not vowing is no sin; God forbids the prophet to pray or intercede for the people, for he will not hear.

leads.title: Jonathan's exploit at Michmash and Saul's rash oath ↔ Talut (Saul), the ark and Jalut (Goliath)
leads.summary: These two units share 1 motifs: it is the same to god to help the many or the powerless.

passages.note: It is the same to God to help the many or the powerless (1Sam 14:6 kî ʾên la-YHWH maʿṣôr lĕhôšîaʿ bĕ-rab ʾô bi-mʿāṭ, said by Jonathan; Q 2:249 kam min fiʾatin qalīlatin ghalabat fiʾatan kathīratan bi-idhni llāhi wa-llāhu maʿa ṣ-ṣābirīn, said by those of Saul's men who expect to meet God. The same maxim in the same war setting (Saul's army against the Philistines).)
passages.text: וַיֹּ֨אמֶר יְהוֹנָתָ֜ן אֶל הַנַּ֣עַר נֹשֵׂ֣א כֵלָ֗יו לְכָה֙ וְנַעְבְּרָ֗ה אֶל מַצַּב֙ הָעֲרֵלִ֣ים הָאֵ֔לֶּה אוּלַ֛י יַעֲשֶׂ֥ה יְהוָ֖ה לָ֑נוּ כִּ֣י אֵ֤ין לַֽיהוָה֙ מַעְצ֔וֹר לְהוֹשִׁ֥יעַ בְּרַ֖ב א֥וֹ בִמְעָֽט

passages.note: It is the same to God to help the many or the powerless
passages.text: فَلَمَّا فَصَلَ طَالُوتُ بِٱلْجُنُودِ قَالَ إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ مُبْتَلِيكُم بِنَهَرٍ فَمَن شَرِبَ مِنْهُ فَلَيْسَ مِنِّى وَمَن لَّمْ يَطْعَمْهُ فَإِنَّهُۥ مِنِّىٓ إِلَّا مَنِ ٱغْتَرَفَ غُرْفَةًۢ بِيَدِهِۦ فَشَرِبُوا۟ مِنْهُ إِلَّا قَلِيلًا مِّنْهُمْ فَلَمَّا جَاوَزَهُۥ هُوَ وَٱلَّذِينَ ءَامَنُوا۟ مَعَهُۥ قَالُوا۟ لَا طَاقَةَ لَنَا ٱلْيَوْمَ بِجَالُوتَ وَجُنُودِهِۦ قَالَ ٱلَّذِينَ يَظُنُّونَ أَنَّهُم مُّلَٰقُوا۟ ٱللَّهِ كَم مِّن فِئَةٍ قَلِيلَةٍ غَلَبَتْ فِئَةً كَثِيرَةًۢ بِإِذْنِ ٱللَّهِ وَٱللَّهُ مَعَ ٱلصَّٰبِرِينَ

evidence.text: Confirmed by a side-by-side reading of both originals (alignments/hb-quran/01-hb-quran.yaml): parallel. 1Sam 14:6 kî ʾên la-YHWH maʿṣôr lĕhôšîaʿ bĕ-rab ʾô bi-mʿāṭ, said by Jonathan; Q 2:249 kam min fiʾatin qalīlatin ghalabat fiʾatan kathīratan bi-idhni llāhi wa-llāhu maʿa ṣ-ṣābirīn, said by those of Saul's men who expect to meet God. The same maxim in the same war setting (Saul's army against the Philistines).
Shared motifs, rarest first: It is the same to God to help the many or the powerless (weight 6.3). Pair score 6.3.

Only in Jonathan's exploit at Michmash and Saul's rash oath: A hero and his armor-bearer alone attack an enemy garrison; Tasting honey makes the hero's eyes brighten; Two named rock crags (Bozez and Seneh) flank a pass; The people ransom the king's condemned son from his father's oath; King curses anyone who eats before evening; his own son unknowingly breaks it; Hero sets a sign: the enemy's words will show whether to advance; People eat meat with the blood; king has a large stone set for proper slaughter; Lot or Urim-Thummim cast to identify the guilty party (tamim); Divine panic and earthquake make the enemy turn swords on one another; List of the king's sons, daughters, wife and commander; A priest or oracle is consulted about the success of an undertaking.

Only in Talut (Saul), the ark and Jalut (Goliath): The ark (tabut) returns, carried by angels, containing tranquility (sakina) and relics left by the family of Moses and Aaron; David kills Jalut (Goliath) and is given kingship and wisdom; Were it not for God checking people by means of others, the earth would be corrupted; 'How many a small band has overcome a large one by God's leave'; God chose the king and increased him in knowledge and stature, though he lacked wealth; The people object that the chosen king has no wealth and they have more right to kingship; Before battle the army is tested at a river: whoever drinks is not with the leader, except a handful scooped by hand; The ark of the covenant: a gold-plated acacia chest with rings and poles [divergence between the texts]; What the ark contains [contrast between the texts]; David kills the Philistine giant [divergence between the texts]; A giant taunts Israel and is killed by a hero; A jar of manna preserved before the testimony for future generations; and 10 more.

evidence.text: Confirmed by a side-by-side reading of both originals (alignments/hb-quran/01-hb-quran.yaml): divergence. 2Chr 6:34, 38 wĕ-hitpallĕlû ʾēlêkā derek hā-ʿîr ha-zzōʾt ʾăšer bāḥartā bāh wĕ-ha-bbayit ʾăšer bānîtî li-šmekā: wherever Israel is (at war, in captivity), they pray toward the chosen city and the house Solomon built; Q 2:144, 150 wa-ḥaythu mā kuntum fa-wallū wujūhakum shaṭrahu: wherever you are, turn your faces toward the Sacred Mosque. Same rule (pray toward the house from wherever you are), new house.

Only in The change of qibla: The direction of prayer (qibla) is changed toward the Sacred Mosque; fools ask why; Believers made a middle community (umma wasat), witnesses over mankind, with the messenger a witness over them; God sees the prophet turning his face toward heaven and grants him a qibla he is pleased with; To each a direction he faces: so race toward good deeds; Abraham and Ishmael pray that a messenger be raised from among their offspring; The People of the Book recognize the truth as they recognize their own sons; Leader prays 'remember me, my God, for good' for his deeds; Who bears witness to God's oneness [divergence between the texts].

evidence.text: Confirmed by a side-by-side reading of both originals (alignments/hb-quran/05-hb-quran.yaml): divergence, parallel. jiʾtuka min Sabaʾin bi-nabaʾin yaqīnin innī wajadtu mraʾatan tamlikuhum ~ û-malkat Šəvāʾ šāməʿâ ʾet šēmaʿ Šəlōmōh wat-tāvôʾ: a woman ruling Sheba (Sabaʾ / Šəvāʾ), a report (nabaʾ / šēmaʿ), and her coming to Solomon. The direction of the report is reversed: in Chronicles she hears of Solomon, in the Quran Solomon hears of her through the hoopoe. Who tests whom: in Chronicles the queen comes to test Solomon with riddles (lənassôt ʾet Šəlōmōh bə-ḥîdôt) and he answers all (wə-lōʾ neʿlam dāvār miš-Šəlōmōh); in the Quran Solomon tests the queen: nakkirū lahā ʿarshahā nanẓur a-tahtadī, and she answers ka-annahu huwa. The gifts: Chronicles has the queen bring 120 talents of gold, spices and gems, which Solomon accepts, and he gives her all she desires (nātan ... ʾet kol ḥefṣāh). In the Quran she sends a gift (hadiyya) to test him, and Solomon refuses it, a-tumiddūnani bi-mālin fa-mā ātāniya llāhu khayrun mimmā ātākum, and threatens to invade with armies they cannot resist. The queen overwhelmed by Solomon's building: Chronicles has her see the house he built (wə-hab-bayit ʾăšer bānâ) until wə-lōʾ hāyâ ʿôd bāh rûaḥ; the Quran has the palace of smooth glass (ṣarḥun mumarradun min qawārīr) that she takes for deep water (ḥasibathu lujjatan) and uncovers her legs. Awe becomes a test she fails and then learns from. cf. Targum Sheni Esther 1:2 (glass floor), outside the HB. The queen's last word: Chronicles has a blessing of Solomon's God, yəhî YHWH ʾĕlōhêkā bārûkh ʾăšer ḥāfēṣ bəkhā lə-tittəkhā ʿal kisʾô, 'your God', praised for Israel's king. The Quran has a conversion: rabbi innī ẓalamtu nafsī wa-aslamtu maʿa Sulaymāna lillāhi rabbi l-ʿālamīn, after the hoopoe reported that she and her people worshipped the sun (27:24). Chronicles never calls her an idolater. The great throne: Chronicles praises Solomon's own (wa-yyaʿaś ham-melekh kissēʾ šēn gādôl wa-yṣappēhû zāhāv ṭāhôr); in the Quran the great throne is the queen's (wa-lahā ʿarshun ʿaẓīmun), and Solomon has it carried to him in the blink of an eye by one with knowledge of the Book.

Shared motifs, rarest first: The queen of Sheba visits Solomon (weight 6.7); The great throne in the Sheba story, and whose it is [divergence between the texts] (weight 6.7); Who tests whom between Solomon and the queen of Sheba [divergence between the texts] (weight 6.7); The queen of Sheba's gifts and Solomon's response [divergence between the texts] (weight 6.7); The queen of Sheba overwhelmed by Solomon's buildings [divergence between the texts] (weight 6.7); A foreign queen tests the king with riddles and he answers them all (weight 6.3); What the queen of Sheba says of Solomon's God [divergence between the texts] (weight 6.3). Pair score 46.0.

Only in The Queen of Sheba tests Solomon; his gold, ivory throne, ships and death: A foreign ruler blesses Israel's God for setting the king on his throne; The king exceeds all the kings of the earth in riches and wisdom; All the kings of Arabia and governors bring gold and silver; An annual income of 666 talents of gold; A visitor says she did not believe the report until she saw: not half was told her; Rare almug wood from Ophir used for temple supports and lyres for singers; never seen again; Promised land stretches from the river of Egypt to the Euphrates; A visitor seeing the king's court is left breathless ('no more spirit in her'); A royal visitor arrives with camels carrying spices, gold and precious stones; Great ivory throne overlaid with gold, with six steps and twelve lions on the steps and two beside the arms; Tarshish ships every three years bring gold, silver, ivory, apes and peacocks (or baboons); Shields of beaten gold made or captured and displayed; and 6 more.

Only in Solomon, the speech of birds, the ants, the hoopoe and the Queen of Sheba: Entering Solomon's palace, the queen takes its floor of smooth glass for a pool and bares her legs; The hoopoe returns with sure news from Sabaʾ, knowledge Solomon lacked; Solomon sends the hoopoe to drop his letter before the queen and wait for their reply; Solomon reviews the birds, finds the hoopoe absent and threatens to punish or slaughter it unless it brings a clear excuse; An ʿifrīt of the jinn offers to bring the queen's throne before Solomon rises from his seat; Solomon's letter begins 'In the name of God, the Merciful, the Compassionate' and demands submission; The queen sends a gift to see what the envoys bring back; Solomon rejects the wealth and threatens invasion; The queen confesses she wronged herself and submits with Solomon to God, Lord of the worlds; Solomon has the queen's throne disguised to test whether she recognizes it; she says 'It is as though it were it'; The queen and her people prostrate to the sun instead of God; Solomon inherits from David (knowledge and kingship); Solomon prays to be inspired to thank God for favor to him and his parents and to be admitted among the righteous; and 16 more.

leads.title: Athaliah's usurpation and the hidden prince Joash ↔ Jehoiada's coup with the Levites; Joash crowned, Athaliah killed, Baal temple destroyed
leads.summary: These two units share 5 motifs: king david's spears and shields kept in the temple are issued to the guards, a priest organizes the guards to overthrow a ruler and enthrone the hidden heir, coronation in which the king receives the crown (nezer) and the 'testimony' (edut), the temple of baal is torn down and its priest slain before the altars….

evidence.text: Confirmed by a side-by-side reading of both originals (alignments/hb-quran/03-hb-quran.yaml): echo. Imitation of the neighbours' gods and the vanity of their cult: wa-bāṭilun mā kānū yaʿmalūn, mutabbarun mā hum fīhi vs wayyēlᵉkû ʾaḥărê hahebel wayyehbālû wᵉʾaḥărê haggôyim ʾăšer sᵉbîbōtām ... lᵉbiltî ʿăśôt kāhem.

Shared motifs, rarest first: After crossing the sea the people see idol-worshipers and ask the prophet for a god like theirs (weight 6.3); People make a molten calf while the leader is on the mountain (weight 4.7). Pair score 11.0.

Only in Fall of Samaria and the sermon on Israel's exile: God warned the people by all his prophets and seers, 'Turn from your evil ways', but they would not listen; Vassal king withholds tribute and seeks help from Egypt, and is imprisoned; Kings or people practice divination (qesem) and augury (nihush); A capital city is besieged for three years before it falls; Theological sermon explaining the fall and exile of a nation as punishment for idolatry; Formula: he did not depart from the sins of Jeroboam son of Nebat who made Israel sin; God calls Israel a stiff-necked people; King makes his son 'pass through the fire' after the abominations of the nations; Idols called 'elilim' ('nothings'); People bow down to all the host of heaven; An Assyrian king named in the narrative (Pul, Tiglath-pileser, Shalmaneser, Sennacherib, Esarhaddon); Conquered population deported to Assyria or another distant land; and 1 more.

Only in Israel asks for a god like the idol-worshipers: Israel asks its leader to make them a god [divergence between the texts]; People demand a king 'like all the nations'; Israel chosen as God's treasured people (am segullah) out of all peoples; Ruler orders the killing of male infants.

leads.title: The resettled peoples, the lions and the syncretistic cult of Samaria ↔ Pagan portions and taboos; eight pairs; what is forbidden to all and to the Jews
leads.summary: These two units share 2 motifs: settlers fear yhwh yet serve their own gods (syncretism), nations burn their sons and daughters in fire to their gods.

passages.note: Settlers fear YHWH yet serve their own gods (syncretism)
passages.text: וַיִּהְי֥וּ יְרֵאִ֖ים אֶת יְהוָ֑ה וַיַּעֲשׂ֨וּ לָהֶ֤ם מִקְצוֹתָם֙ כֹּהֲנֵ֣י בָמ֔וֹת וַיִּהְי֛וּ עֹשִׂ֥ים לָהֶ֖ם בְּבֵ֥ית הַבָּמֽוֹת

passages.note: Settlers fear YHWH yet serve their own gods (syncretism)
passages.text: אֶת יְהוָ֖ה הָי֣וּ יְרֵאִ֑ים וְאֶת אֱלֹֽהֵיהֶם֙ הָי֣וּ עֹֽבְדִ֔ים כְּמִשְׁפַּט֙ הַגּוֹיִ֔ם אֲשֶׁר הִגְל֥וּ אֹתָ֖ם מִשָּֽׁם

passages.note: Settlers fear YHWH yet serve their own gods (syncretism) (Dividing worship between God and other gods. 2Kgs: ʾet-YHWH hāyû yərēʾîm wə-ʾet-ʾĕlōhêhem hāyû ʿōvədîm. Q: wa-jaʿalū li-llāhi mimmā dharaʾa mina l-ḥarthi wa-l-anʿāmi naṣīban fa-qālū hādhā li-llāhi ... wa-hādhā li-shurakāʾinā. Q adds that God's share ends up going to the partners.)
passages.text: وَجَعَلُوا۟ لِلَّهِ مِمَّا ذَرَأَ مِنَ ٱلْحَرْثِ وَٱلْأَنْعَٰمِ نَصِيبًا فَقَالُوا۟ هَٰذَا لِلَّهِ بِزَعْمِهِمْ وَهَٰذَا لِشُرَكَآئِنَا فَمَا كَانَ لِشُرَكَآئِهِمْ فَلَا يَصِلُ إِلَى ٱللَّهِ وَمَا كَانَ لِلَّهِ فَهُوَ يَصِلُ إِلَىٰ شُرَكَآئِهِمْ سَآءَ مَا يَحْكُمُونَ

passages.note: Nations burn their sons and daughters in fire to their gods (Sepharvites to Adrammelech and Anammelech)
passages.text: וְהָעַוִּ֛ים עָשׂ֥וּ נִבְחַ֖ז וְאֶת תַּרְתָּ֑ק וְהַסְפַרְוִ֗ים שֹׂרְפִ֤ים אֶת בְּנֵיהֶם֙ בָּאֵ֔שׁ לְאַדְרַמֶּ֥לֶךְ וַֽעֲנַמֶּ֖לֶךְ אלה אֱלֹהֵ֥י ספרים סְפַרְוָֽיִם

passages.note: Nations burn their sons and daughters in fire to their gods (the partners made killing their children seem fair to them)
passages.text: وَكَذَٰلِكَ زَيَّنَ لِكَثِيرٍ مِّنَ ٱلْمُشْرِكِينَ قَتْلَ أَوْلَٰدِهِمْ شُرَكَآؤُهُمْ لِيُرْدُوهُمْ وَلِيَلْبِسُوا۟ عَلَيْهِمْ دِينَهُمْ وَلَوْ شَآءَ ٱللَّهُ مَا فَعَلُوهُ فَذَرْهُمْ وَمَا يَفْتَرُونَ

passages.note: Nations burn their sons and daughters in fire to their gods (the partners made killing their children seem fair to them)
passages.text: قَدْ خَسِرَ ٱلَّذِينَ قَتَلُوٓا۟ أَوْلَٰدَهُمْ سَفَهًۢا بِغَيْرِ عِلْمٍ وَحَرَّمُوا۟ مَا رَزَقَهُمُ ٱللَّهُ ٱفْتِرَآءً عَلَى ٱللَّهِ قَدْ ضَلُّوا۟ وَمَا كَانُوا۟ مُهْتَدِينَ

evidence.text: Confirmed by a side-by-side reading of both originals (alignments/hb-quran/02-hb-quran.yaml): parallel. Dividing worship between God and other gods. 2Kgs: ʾet-YHWH hāyû yərēʾîm wə-ʾet-ʾĕlōhêhem hāyû ʿōvədîm. Q: wa-jaʿalū li-llāhi mimmā dharaʾa mina l-ḥarthi wa-l-anʿāmi naṣīban fa-qālū hādhā li-llāhi ... wa-hādhā li-shurakāʾinā. Q adds that God's share ends up going to the partners.
Shared motifs, rarest first: Settlers fear YHWH yet serve their own gods (syncretism) (weight 6.7); Nations burn their sons and daughters in fire to their gods (weight 5.2). Pair score 11.9.

Only in The resettled peoples, the lions and the syncretistic cult of Samaria: Catalogue of foreign gods brought by settler peoples (Succoth-benoth, Nergal, Ashima, Nibhaz, Tartak, Adrammelech, Anammelech); Each land has a god whose 'manner' (mishpat) newcomers must learn; God sends lions to kill settlers who do not know the 'law of the god of the land'; Empire settles foreign peoples in the cities of a deported population; A deported priest is sent back to teach the settlers how to fear the local god; Mutual declaration: Israel avows YHWH as God, YHWH avows Israel as his treasured people.

Only in Pagan portions and taboos; eight pairs; what is forbidden to all and to the Jews: Pagans set apart cattle whose backs may not be ridden or burdened; Eight in pairs: sheep, goats, camels and cattle, male and female; which did God forbid?; Idolaters say 'had God willed we would not have associated partners nor forbidden anything'; Give its due on the day of harvest; For the Jews God forbade every animal with claws/undivided hoof and the fat of cattle and sheep except on backs, entrails or bone; Do not be wasteful; God does not love the wasteful (musrifīn); Pagans assign a portion of crops and cattle to God and a portion to their partners; Pagans declare certain cattle and crops taboo (ḥijr), to be eaten only by whom they will; Pagans reserve what is in the wombs of cattle for males, forbidden to wives unless stillborn; The camel is unclean because it does not have a split hoof [contrast between the texts]; List of clean and unclean animals: split hoof and chewing cud [response between the texts]; The fat tail of the sheep is offered [divergence between the texts]; and 11 more.

evidence.text: Passages are shown for the 10 rarest of 12 shared motifs; the full list follows.

Shared motifs, rarest first: Each man under his own vine and fig tree, drinking from his own cistern (weight 6.7); Invader promises deportees a land like their own, of grain, wine, oil and honey (weight 6.7); Officials ask the envoy to speak Aramaic, not Judean, so the people on the wall will not understand (weight 6.7); Invader claims the defenders' own god sent him to destroy the land (weight 6.7); The people keep silent and do not answer the enemy at the king's command (weight 6.7); Enemy envoy addresses the besieged at the city wall to break their morale (weight 6.7); Egypt likened to a broken reed staff that pierces the hand of whoever leans on it (weight 6.3); Threat that the besieged will eat their own dung and drink their urine (weight 6.3); Taunt: Where are the gods of the conquered nations? Could they save their lands from my hand? (weight 5.8); An Assyrian king named in the narrative (Pul, Tiglath-pileser, Shalmaneser, Sennacherib, Esarhaddon) (weight 5.6); Command to smash altars, standing stones and Asherah poles and burn idols (weight 5.3); Men tear their garments in grief or dismay (weight 4.9). Pair score 74.3.

Only in Hezekiah's reform; Sennacherib's invasion and the Rabshakeh's speech: King smashes the bronze serpent made by Moses, called Nehushtan, because people burned incense to it; Image of a serpent on a pole heals those who look at it; Formula: there was none like him among all the kings before or after; A capital city is besieged for three years before it falls; King strips the temple and palace treasuries to buy off an invader; Conquered population deported to Assyria or another distant land.

Only in Sennacherib's invasion; the Rabshakeh's speech at the conduit: Prophet meets the king at the conduit of the upper pool on the highway of the Fuller's Field; Judah (or allies) put trust in Egypt and Cush for help against Assyria and are put to shame.
