passages.text: שִׁשָּׁה֙ מִשְּׁמֹתָ֔ם עַ֖ל הָאֶ֣בֶן הָאֶחָ֑ת וְאֶת שְׁמ֞וֹת הַשִּׁשָּׁ֧ה הַנּוֹתָרִ֛ים עַל הָאֶ֥בֶן הַשֵּׁנִ֖ית כְּתוֹלְדֹתָֽם

passages.note: The names of the twelve tribes are engraved like seals on gemstones
passages.text: וַֽיַּעֲשׂוּ֙ אֶת אַבְנֵ֣י הַשֹּׁ֔הַם מֻֽסַבֹּ֖ת מִשְׁבְּצֹ֣ת זָהָ֑ב מְפֻתָּחֹת֙ פִּתּוּחֵ֣י חוֹתָ֔ם עַל שְׁמ֖וֹת בְּנֵ֥י יִשְׂרָאֵֽל

passages.note: The names of the twelve tribes are engraved like seals on gemstones
passages.text: וְ֠הָאֲבָנִים עַל שְׁמֹ֨ת בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵ֥ל הֵ֛נָּה שְׁתֵּ֥ים עֶשְׂרֵ֖ה עַל שְׁמֹתָ֑ם פִּתּוּחֵ֤י חֹתָם֙ אִ֣ישׁ עַל שְׁמ֔וֹ לִשְׁנֵ֥ים עָשָׂ֖ר שָֽׁבֶט

passages.note: The robe's neck opening is bound so it will not tear (like the opening of a coat of mail (tahra))
passages.text: וְהָיָ֥ה פִֽי רֹאשׁ֖וֹ בְּתוֹכ֑וֹ שָׂפָ֡ה יִֽהְיֶה֩ לְפִ֨יו סָבִ֜יב מַעֲשֵׂ֣ה אֹרֵ֗ג כְּפִ֥י תַחְרָ֛א יִֽהְיֶה לּ֖וֹ לֹ֥א יִקָּרֵֽעַ

passages.note: The robe's neck opening is bound so it will not tear
passages.text: וּפִֽי הַמְּעִ֥יל בְּתוֹכ֖וֹ כְּפִ֣י תַחְרָ֑א שָׂפָ֥ה לְפִ֛יו סָבִ֖יב לֹ֥א יִקָּרֵֽעַ

passages.note: The priest carries Israel's names before God as a memorial
passages.text: וְשַׂמְתָּ֞ אֶת שְׁתֵּ֣י הָאֲבָנִ֗ים עַ֚ל כִּתְפֹ֣ת הָֽאֵפֹ֔ד אַבְנֵ֥י זִכָּרֹ֖ן לִבְנֵ֣י יִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל וְנָשָׂא֩ אַהֲרֹ֨ן אֶת שְׁמוֹתָ֜ם לִפְנֵ֧י יְהוָ֛ה עַל שְׁתֵּ֥י כְתֵפָ֖יו לְזִכָּרֹֽן

passages.note: The priest carries Israel's names before God as a memorial
passages.text: וְנָשָׂ֣א אַ֠הֲרֹן אֶת שְׁמ֨וֹת בְּנֵֽי יִשְׂרָאֵ֜ל בְּחֹ֧שֶׁן הַמִּשְׁפָּ֛ט עַל לִבּ֖וֹ בְּבֹא֣וֹ אֶל הַקֹּ֑דֶשׁ לְזִכָּרֹ֥ן לִפְנֵֽי יְהוָ֖ה תָּמִֽיד

passages.note: The priest carries Israel's names before God as a memorial
passages.text: וַיָּ֣שֶׂם אֹתָ֗ם עַ֚ל כִּתְפֹ֣ת הָאֵפֹ֔ד אַבְנֵ֥י זִכָּר֖וֹן לִבְנֵ֣י יִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל כַּאֲשֶׁ֛ר צִוָּ֥ה יְהוָ֖ה אֶת מֹשֶֽׁה

passages.note: The priest's robe has gold bells and pomegranates on its hem so he does not die (sound heard so he will not die)
passages.text: (28:31) וְעָשִׂ֛יתָ אֶת מְעִ֥יל הָאֵפ֖וֹד כְּלִ֥יל תְּכֵֽלֶת (28:32) וְהָיָ֥ה פִֽי רֹאשׁ֖וֹ בְּתוֹכ֑וֹ שָׂפָ֡ה יִֽהְיֶה֩ לְפִ֨יו סָבִ֜יב מַעֲשֵׂ֣ה אֹרֵ֗ג כְּפִ֥י תַחְרָ֛א יִֽהְיֶה לּ֖וֹ לֹ֥א יִקָּרֵֽעַ (28:33) וְעָשִׂ֣יתָ עַל שׁוּלָ֗יו רִמֹּנֵי֙ תְּכֵ֤לֶת וְאַרְגָּמָן֙ וְתוֹלַ֣עַת שָׁנִ֔י עַל שׁוּלָ֖יו סָבִ֑יב וּפַעֲמֹנֵ֥י זָהָ֛ב בְּתוֹכָ֖ם סָבִֽיב (28:34) פַּעֲמֹ֤ן זָהָב֙ וְרִמּ֔וֹן פַּֽעֲמֹ֥ן זָהָ֖ב וְרִמּ֑וֹן עַל שׁוּלֵ֥י הַמְּעִ֖יל סָבִֽיב (28:35) וְהָיָ֥ה עַֽל אַהֲרֹ֖ן לְשָׁרֵ֑ת וְנִשְׁמַ֣ע ק֠וֹלוֹ בְּבֹא֨וֹ אֶל הַקֹּ֜דֶשׁ לִפְנֵ֧י יְהוָ֛ה וּבְצֵאת֖וֹ וְלֹ֥א יָמֽוּת

passages.note: The priest's robe has gold bells and pomegranates on its hem so he does not die
passages.text: (39:22) וַיַּ֛עַשׂ אֶת מְעִ֥יל הָאֵפֹ֖ד מַעֲשֵׂ֣ה אֹרֵ֑ג כְּלִ֖יל תְּכֵֽלֶת (39:23) וּפִֽי הַמְּעִ֥יל בְּתוֹכ֖וֹ כְּפִ֣י תַחְרָ֑א שָׂפָ֥ה לְפִ֛יו סָבִ֖יב לֹ֥א יִקָּרֵֽעַ (39:24) וַֽיַּעֲשׂוּ֙ עַל שׁוּלֵ֣י הַמְּעִ֔יל רִמּוֹנֵ֕י תְּכֵ֥לֶת וְאַרְגָּמָ֖ן וְתוֹלַ֣עַת שָׁנִ֑י מָשְׁזָֽר (39:25) וַיַּעֲשׂ֥וּ פַעֲמֹנֵ֖י זָהָ֣ב טָה֑וֹר וַיִּתְּנ֨וּ אֶת הַפַּֽעֲמֹנִ֜ים בְּת֣וֹךְ הָרִמֹּנִ֗ים עַל שׁוּלֵ֤י הַמְּעִיל֙ סָבִ֔יב בְּת֖וֹךְ הָרִמֹּנִֽים (39:26) פַּעֲמֹ֤ן וְרִמֹּן֙ פַּעֲמֹ֣ן וְרִמֹּ֔ן עַל שׁוּלֵ֥י הַמְּעִ֖יל סָבִ֑יב לְשָׁרֵ֕ת כַּאֲשֶׁ֛ר צִוָּ֥ה יְהוָ֖ה אֶת מֹשֶֽׁה

passages.note: The ephod, a woven priestly garment with shoulder pieces
passages.text: (28:6) וְעָשׂ֖וּ אֶת הָאֵפֹ֑ד זָ֠הָב תְּכֵ֨לֶת וְאַרְגָּמָ֜ן תּוֹלַ֧עַת שָׁנִ֛י וְשֵׁ֥שׁ מָשְׁזָ֖ר מַעֲשֵׂ֥ה חֹשֵֽׁב (28:7) שְׁתֵּ֧י כְתֵפֹ֣ת חֹֽבְרֹ֗ת יִֽהְיֶה לּ֛וֹ אֶל שְׁנֵ֥י קְצוֹתָ֖יו וְחֻבָּֽר (28:8) וְחֵ֤שֶׁב אֲפֻדָּתוֹ֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר עָלָ֔יו כְּמַעֲשֵׂ֖הוּ מִמֶּ֣נּוּ יִהְיֶ֑ה זָהָ֗ב תְּכֵ֧לֶת וְאַרְגָּמָ֛ן וְתוֹלַ֥עַת שָׁנִ֖י וְשֵׁ֥שׁ מָשְׁזָֽר (28:9) וְלָ֣קַחְתָּ֔ אֶת שְׁתֵּ֖י אַבְנֵי שֹׁ֑הַם וּפִתַּחְתָּ֣ עֲלֵיהֶ֔ם שְׁמ֖וֹת בְּנֵ֥י יִשְׂרָאֵֽל (28:10) שִׁשָּׁה֙ מִשְּׁמֹתָ֔ם עַ֖ל הָאֶ֣בֶן הָאֶחָ֑ת וְאֶת שְׁמ֞וֹת הַשִּׁשָּׁ֧ה הַנּוֹתָרִ֛ים עַל הָאֶ֥בֶן הַשֵּׁנִ֖ית כְּתוֹלְדֹתָֽם (28:11) מַעֲשֵׂ֣ה חָרַשׁ֮ אֶבֶן֒ פִּתּוּחֵ֣י חֹתָ֗ם תְּפַתַּח֙ אֶת שְׁתֵּ֣י הָאֲבָנִ֔ים עַל שְׁמֹ֖ת בְּנֵ֣י יִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל מֻסַבֹּ֛ת מִשְׁבְּצ֥וֹת זָהָ֖ב תַּעֲשֶׂ֥ה אֹתָֽם (28:12) וְשַׂמְתָּ֞ אֶת שְׁתֵּ֣י הָאֲבָנִ֗ים עַ֚ל כִּתְפֹ֣ת הָֽאֵפֹ֔ד אַבְנֵ֥י זִכָּרֹ֖ן לִבְנֵ֣י יִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל וְנָשָׂא֩ אַהֲרֹ֨ן אֶת שְׁמוֹתָ֜ם לִפְנֵ֧י יְהוָ֛ה עַל שְׁתֵּ֥י כְתֵפָ֖יו לְזִכָּרֹֽן (28:13) וְעָשִׂ֥יתָ מִשְׁבְּצֹ֖ת זָהָֽב (28:14) וּשְׁתֵּ֤י שַׁרְשְׁרֹת֙ זָהָ֣ב טָה֔וֹר מִגְבָּלֹ֛ת תַּעֲשֶׂ֥ה אֹתָ֖ם מַעֲשֵׂ֣ה עֲבֹ֑ת וְנָתַתָּ֛ה אֶת שַׁרְשְׁרֹ֥ת הָעֲבֹתֹ֖ת עַל הַֽמִּשְׁבְּצֹֽת

passages.note: The ephod, a woven priestly garment with shoulder pieces
passages.text: (39:2) וַיַּ֖עַשׂ אֶת הָאֵפֹ֑ד זָהָ֗ב תְּכֵ֧לֶת וְאַרְגָּמָ֛ן וְתוֹלַ֥עַת שָׁנִ֖י וְשֵׁ֥שׁ מָשְׁזָֽר (39:3) וַֽיְרַקְּע֞וּ אֶת פַּחֵ֣י הַזָּהָב֮ וְקִצֵּ֣ץ פְּתִילִם֒ לַעֲשׂ֗וֹת בְּת֤וֹךְ הַתְּכֵ֨לֶת֙ וּבְת֣וֹךְ הָֽאַרְגָּמָ֔ן וּבְת֛וֹךְ תּוֹלַ֥עַת הַשָּׁנִ֖י וּבְת֣וֹךְ הַשֵּׁ֑שׁ מַעֲשֵׂ֖ה חֹשֵֽׁב (39:4) כְּתֵפֹ֥ת עָֽשׂוּ ל֖וֹ חֹבְרֹ֑ת עַל שְׁנֵ֥י קצוותו קְצוֹתָ֖יו חֻבָּֽר (39:5) וְחֵ֨שֶׁב אֲפֻדָּת֜וֹ אֲשֶׁ֣ר עָלָ֗יו מִמֶּ֣נּוּ הוּא֮ כְּמַעֲשֵׂהוּ֒ זָהָ֗ב תְּכֵ֧לֶת וְאַרְגָּמָ֛ן וְתוֹלַ֥עַת שָׁנִ֖י וְשֵׁ֣שׁ מָשְׁזָ֑ר כַּאֲשֶׁ֛ר צִוָּ֥ה יְהוָ֖ה אֶת מֹשֶֽׁה

passages.note: The breastpiece of judgment set with twelve gems in four rows (four rows: odem, pitdah, bareqet / nofekh, sappir, yahalom / leshem, shevo, ahlamah / tarshish, shoham, yashfeh)
passages.text: (28:15) וְעָשִׂ֜יתָ חֹ֤שֶׁן מִשְׁפָּט֙ מַעֲשֵׂ֣ה חֹשֵׁ֔ב כְּמַעֲשֵׂ֥ה אֵפֹ֖ד תַּעֲשֶׂ֑נּוּ זָ֠הָב תְּכֵ֨לֶת וְאַרְגָּמָ֜ן וְתוֹלַ֧עַת שָׁנִ֛י וְשֵׁ֥שׁ מָשְׁזָ֖ר תַּעֲשֶׂ֥ה אֹתֽוֹ (28:16) רָב֥וּעַ יִֽהְיֶ֖ה כָּפ֑וּל זֶ֥רֶת אָרְכּ֖וֹ וְזֶ֥רֶת רָחְבּֽוֹ (28:17) וּמִלֵּאתָ֥ בוֹ֙ מִלֻּ֣אַת אֶ֔בֶן אַרְבָּעָ֖ה טוּרִ֣ים אָ֑בֶן ט֗וּר אֹ֤דֶם פִּטְדָה֙ וּבָרֶ֔קֶת הַטּ֖וּר הָאֶחָֽד (28:18) וְהַטּ֖וּר הַשֵּׁנִ֑י נֹ֥פֶךְ סַפִּ֖יר וְיָהֲלֹֽם (28:19) וְהַטּ֖וּר הַשְּׁלִישִׁ֑י לֶ֥שֶׁם שְׁב֖וֹ וְאַחְלָֽמָה (28:20) וְהַטּוּר֙ הָרְבִיעִ֔י תַּרְשִׁ֥ישׁ וְשֹׁ֖הַם וְיָשְׁפֵ֑ה מְשֻׁבָּצִ֥ים זָהָ֛ב יִהְי֖וּ בְּמִלּוּאֹתָֽם (28:21) וְ֠הָאֲבָנִים תִּֽהְיֶ֜יןָ עַל שְׁמֹ֧ת בְּנֵֽי יִשְׂרָאֵ֛ל שְׁתֵּ֥ים עֶשְׂרֵ֖ה עַל שְׁמֹתָ֑ם פִּתּוּחֵ֤י חוֹתָם֙ אִ֣ישׁ עַל שְׁמ֔וֹ תִּֽהְיֶ֕יןָ לִשְׁנֵ֥י עָשָׂ֖ר שָֽׁבֶט

passages.note: The breastpiece of judgment set with twelve gems in four rows
passages.text_omitted: longer than 12 verses; read it in the source

passages.note: Priests wear linen breeches to cover their nakedness, on pain of death
passages.text: וַעֲשֵׂ֤ה לָהֶם֙ מִכְנְסֵי בָ֔ד לְכַסּ֖וֹת בְּשַׂ֣ר עֶרְוָ֑ה מִמָּתְנַ֥יִם וְעַד יְרֵכַ֖יִם יִהְיֽוּ

passages.note: Priests wear linen breeches to cover their nakedness, on pain of death
passages.text: וְהָיוּ֩ עַל אַהֲרֹ֨ן וְעַל בָּנָ֜יו בְּבֹאָ֣ם אֶל אֹ֣הֶל מוֹעֵ֗ד א֣וֹ בְגִשְׁתָּ֤ם אֶל הַמִּזְבֵּ֨חַ֙ לְשָׁרֵ֣ת בַּקֹּ֔דֶשׁ וְלֹא יִשְׂא֥וּ עָוֺ֖ן וָמֵ֑תוּ חֻקַּ֥ת עוֹלָ֛ם ל֖וֹ וּלְזַרְע֥וֹ אַחֲרָֽיו

passages.note: Priests wear linen breeches to cover their nakedness, on pain of death
passages.text: וְאֵת֙ הַמִּצְנֶ֣פֶת שֵׁ֔שׁ וְאֶת פַּאֲרֵ֥י הַמִּגְבָּעֹ֖ת שֵׁ֑שׁ וְאֶת מִכְנְסֵ֥י הַבָּ֖ד שֵׁ֥שׁ מָשְׁזָֽר

passages.note: A gold plate engraved 'Holy to YHWH' on the priest's forehead (on forehead; bears the iniquity of the holy things)
passages.text: וְעָשִׂ֥יתָ צִּ֖יץ זָהָ֣ב טָה֑וֹר וּפִתַּחְתָּ֤ עָלָיו֙ פִּתּוּחֵ֣י חֹתָ֔ם קֹ֖דֶשׁ לַֽיהוָֽה

passages.note: A gold plate engraved 'Holy to YHWH' on the priest's forehead (on forehead; bears the iniquity of the holy things)

passages.text: וַיִּתְּנ֤וּ עָלָיו֙ פְּתִ֣יל תְּכֵ֔לֶת לָתֵ֥ת עַל הַמִּצְנֶ֖פֶת מִלְמָ֑עְלָה כַּאֲשֶׁ֛ר צִוָּ֥ה יְהוָ֖ה אֶת מֹשֶֽׁה

evidence.text: Shared motifs, rarest first: The names of the twelve tribes are engraved like seals on gemstones (weight 6.7); The robe's neck opening is bound so it will not tear (weight 6.7); The priest carries Israel's names before God as a memorial (weight 6.7); The priest's robe has gold bells and pomegranates on its hem so he does not die (weight 6.7); The ephod, a woven priestly garment with shoulder pieces (weight 6.3); The breastpiece of judgment set with twelve gems in four rows (weight 6.3); Priests wear linen breeches to cover their nakedness, on pain of death (weight 6.3); A gold plate engraved 'Holy to YHWH' on the priest's forehead (weight 6.0). Pair score 51.6.

Only in The high priest's vestments: Aaron and his sons are designated as priests; Priestly garments are made for glory and beauty; Priests are installed by anointing and 'filling the hand'; Urim and Thummim placed in the breastpiece for divine decision; God fills craftsmen with a spirit of wisdom for sacred work.

Only in The vestments made; the work completed and blessed: Gold is beaten into sheets and cut into threads for weaving; The leader sees the finished work and blesses the workers; Completion of the sanctuary is narrated in the language of the completion of creation; The refrain 'as YHWH commanded Moses' recurs in a sevenfold pattern; Execution of a divine command is narrated by repeating the command almost verbatim.

leads.title: Ordination of the priests ↔ Moses ordains Aaron and his sons
leads.summary: These two units share 10 motifs: anointing oil is poured on the head of the priest, blood and anointing oil are sprinkled on the priests and their garments, ordination of priests lasts seven days, portions are waved before god as a wave offering….

evidence.text: Shared motifs, rarest first: Anointing oil is poured on the head of the priest (weight 6.7); Blood and anointing oil are sprinkled on the priests and their garments (weight 6.7); Ordination of priests lasts seven days (weight 6.7); Portions are waved before God as a wave offering (weight 6.3); Priests are washed with water at the entrance before ordination (weight 6.3); Blood is daubed on the right earlobe, thumb and big toe (weight 6.3); Sacred meat left over until morning is burned (weight 6.3); The offerer lays his hand on the head of the animal (weight 5.8); The flesh, skin and dung of the sin offering are burned outside the camp (weight 5.8); Blood is put on the horns of the altar with the finger and poured at its base (weight 5.8). Pair score 62.5.

Only in Ordination of the priests: A basket of unleavened bread, oiled cakes and wafers is offered; An outsider may not eat holy food; The high priest's vestments pass to his successor, who wears them seven days; The breast and the right thigh are the priests' portion; Sacrificial animals must be without blemish; Whatever touches the most holy altar or holy things becomes holy; An offering by fire is a pleasing odor to God; The fat, the two kidneys and the lobe of the liver are burned on the altar; The fat tail of the sheep is offered.

Only in Moses ordains Aaron and his sons: Moses himself performs the priestly rites at the ordination; The whole congregation is assembled at the tent entrance to witness a rite; Anointing makes the tent and its furnishings holy; The refrain 'as YHWH commanded Moses' recurs in a sevenfold pattern; The ephod, a woven priestly garment with shoulder pieces; Urim and Thummim placed in the breastpiece for divine decision; Execution of a divine command is narrated by repeating the command almost verbatim; A gold plate engraved 'Holy to YHWH' on the priest's forehead; A ritual action is performed seven times.

leads.title: The burning bush and the divine name ↔ Moses, Ishmael and Idris remembered; the later generation that neglected prayer (Surah 19:51-65)
leads.summary: These two units share 1 motifs: god called moses and drew him near in confidential converse (najiyy) [divergence between the texts].

evidence.text: Confirmed by a side-by-side reading of both originals (alignments/hb-quran/04-hb-quran.yaml): divergence, parallel. Setting and motive change. Exod: Moses alone with Jethro's flock at har hāʾĕlōhîm, drawn by a wonder, hassəneh bōʿēr bāʾēš wəhassəneh ʾênennû ʾukkāl ... ʾāsurâ-nnāʾ wəʾerʾeh. Q: Moses traveling with his family (qāla li-ahlihi mkuthū) sees a fire and goes for a practical need, la-ʿallī ātīkum minhā bi-qabasin aw ajidu ʿalā n-nāri hudā. Q 20 does not mention the unconsumed bush. šal-nəʿālêkā mēʿal raglêkā kî hammāqôm ʾăšer ʾattâ ʿômēd ʿālāyw ʾadmat-qōdeš hûʾ; fa-khlaʿ naʿlayka innaka bi-l-wādi l-muqaddasi Ṭuwā: same command, same reason (qōdeš / muqaddas). Q names the place Ṭuwā. God's self-introduction. Exod: ancestral God and the revealed name, ʾānōkî ʾĕlōhê ʾābîkā ʾĕlōhê ʾabrāhām ... ʾehyeh ʾăšer ʾehyeh ... YHWH ʾĕlōhê ʾăbōtêkem ... zeh-ššəmî ləʿōlām. Q: universal confession and worship, innī ana rabbuka ... innanī ana llāhu lā ilāha illā ana fa-ʿbudnī wa-aqimi ṣ-ṣalāta li-dhikrī. No patriarchs and no special name, and prayer is commanded. Q adds the Hour (20:15).

Shared motifs, rarest first: Traveling with his family, the prophet sees a fire and goes to bring back a brand or find guidance there [divergence between the texts] (weight 6.7); A shepherd tending flocks comes to the mountain of God and is called (weight 6.3); The call comes in the holy valley named Ṭuwā [divergence between the texts] (weight 6.3); Hero told to remove his sandals because the place is holy ground (weight 6.3); God appears in a bush that burns without being consumed (weight 6.0). Pair score 31.5.

Only in The burning bush and the divine name: God names himself 'I will be what I will be' (ehyeh asher ehyeh); God has seen the affliction, heard the cry and comes down to deliver; God introduced to a foreign king as 'the God of the Hebrews'; God foretells that the king will not let the people go except under compulsion; Hero hides his face, afraid to look at God; The sign confirming the call is that the people will later worship on this mountain; God calls Moses from the fire, from a bush or a tree [divergence between the texts]; God declares his name as his everlasting memorial for all generations; The title of God in whose name Moses goes to Pharaoh; The list of fathers in 'God of your fathers' [divergence between the texts]; Whose forefathers' God is proclaimed in the Moses story [divergence between the texts]; How God names himself to Moses from the fire [divergence between the texts]; and 13 more.

Only in Moses at the fire in the holy valley Tuwa: The Hour is coming; God almost keeps it hidden so each soul is repaid for its striving; Prophet prays for his chest to be expanded and the knot of his tongue untied; Asked what is in his hand, the prophet lists his staff's uses: leaning, beating down leaves for sheep, other needs; The prophet asks that his brother be made his helper (wazīr) and partner in his mission; The prophet asks that his brother be made his helper (wazīr) and partner in his mission [divergence between the texts]; The call comes in the holy valley named Ṭuwā; Asked what is in his hand, the prophet lists his staff's uses: leaning, beating down leaves for sheep, other needs [divergence between the texts]; Prophet protests he is heavy of mouth and tongue or 'uncircumcised of lips' [divergence between the texts]; Prophet's hand turns leprous, white as snow, and is restored as a sign [divergence between the texts]; Traveling with his family, the prophet sees a fire and goes to bring back a brand or find guidance there; An eloquent brother is appointed to speak for the hero, who is 'as God' to him; Prophet's hand turns leprous, white as snow, and is restored as a sign; and 3 more.

evidence.text: Confirmed by a side-by-side reading of both originals (alignments/hb-quran/05-hb-quran.yaml): divergence, parallel. innī ānastu nāran ... fa-lammā jāʾahā nūdiya an būrika man fī n-nāri wa-man ḥawlahā ~ wa-yyērāʾ malʾakh YHWH ʾēlāyw bə-labbat ʾēš mit-tôkh has-səneh ... wa-yyiqrāʾ ʾēlāyw ʾĕlōhîm mit-tôkh has-səneh: Moses approaches a fire and is called from within it. The Quran does not mention the bush (only 'who is in the fire and around it'), nor the bush not being consumed. Why Moses goes to the fire: Exodus has him alone with Jethro's flock at Horeb, turning aside to see the great sight (ʾāsurâ nāʾ wə-ʾerʾeh ʾet ham-marʾeh hag-gādōl haz-zeh); the Quran has him traveling with his family (qāla Mūsā li-ahlihi), going to bring back news or a burning brand 'that you may warm yourselves'. The Quran names neither flock, mountain nor Jethro. God's self-identification from the fire: Exodus has ʾānōkhî ʾĕlōhê ʾāvîkā ʾĕlōhê ʾAvrāhām ʾĕlōhê Yiṣḥāq wē-ʾlōhê Yaʿăqōv, then ʾehyeh ʾăšer ʾehyeh; the Quran has yā Mūsā innahu ana llāhu l-ʿazīzu l-ḥakīmu, preceded by subḥāna llāhi rabbi l-ʿālamīna. The God of the fathers becomes the Lord of the worlds, and the name-riddle becomes 'Allāh'. The Quran also leaves out the sandals and Moses hiding his face (Exod 3:5-6).

Shared motifs, rarest first: Why Moses approaches the fire [divergence between the texts] (weight 6.7); How God names himself to Moses from the fire [divergence between the texts] (weight 6.7); God appears in a bush that burns without being consumed (weight 6.0). Pair score 19.4.

Only in The burning bush and the divine name: God names himself 'I will be what I will be' (ehyeh asher ehyeh); God has seen the affliction, heard the cry and comes down to deliver; God introduced to a foreign king as 'the God of the Hebrews'; God foretells that the king will not let the people go except under compulsion; Hero hides his face, afraid to look at God; The sign confirming the call is that the people will later worship on this mountain; God calls Moses from the fire, from a bush or a tree [divergence between the texts]; God declares his name as his everlasting memorial for all generations; The title of God in whose name Moses goes to Pharaoh; The list of fathers in 'God of your fathers' [divergence between the texts]; Whose forefathers' God is proclaimed in the Moses story [divergence between the texts]; Formulaic list of the Canaanite, Hittite, Amorite, Perizzite, Hivite and Jebusite; and 15 more.

Only in Ta Sin; Moses at the fire, the jann-staff and the nine signs: At the fire the voice proclaims 'Blessed is he who is in the fire and those around it'; God described as the one who dwells in the bush (seneh); Moses was given nine clear signs; The number of signs or plagues in Egypt [divergence between the texts]; The thrown staff quivers like a jānn (small snake) and Moses turns and flees without looking back; Moses flees from his staff turned serpent, and God's response [divergence between the texts]; Traveling with his family, the prophet sees a fire and goes to bring back a brand or find guidance there; Why Pharaoh and Egypt refuse despite the signs [divergence between the texts]; Moses' hand turned white as a sign [divergence between the texts]; A poetic list of the Egyptian plagues differs in number and order from Exodus; Prophet's hand turns leprous, white as snow, and is restored as a sign; A staff thrown down becomes a serpent and turns back into a staff; and 4 more.

leads.summary: These two units share 4 motifs: where and how moses comes to the place of his call [divergence between the texts], god calls moses from the fire, from a bush or a tree [divergence between the texts], a shepherd tending flocks comes to the mountain of god and is called, god appears in a bush that burns without being consumed.

passages.note: Where and how Moses comes to the place of his call [divergence between the texts] (Place and occasion of the call: Exodus has Moses shepherding Jethro's flock 'behind the wilderness' to Horeb, the mountain of God, a place of holy ground (ʾadmat qōdeš hûʾ), where he must take off his sandals. The Quran has Moses, after completing his term (qaḍā Mūsā l-ajala), traveling with his family, seeing fire on the side of the Mount (jānib aṭ-Ṭūr), and called from the right bank of the valley in 'the blessed spot' (al-buqʿa al-mubāraka). There are no flock and no sandals; the holy ground becomes a blessed spot.)

evidence.text: Confirmed by a side-by-side reading of both originals (alignments/hb-quran/05-hb-quran.yaml): divergence. Place and occasion of the call: Exodus has Moses shepherding Jethro's flock 'behind the wilderness' to Horeb, the mountain of God, a place of holy ground (ʾadmat qōdeš hûʾ), where he must take off his sandals. The Quran has Moses, after completing his term (qaḍā Mūsā l-ajala), traveling with his family, seeing fire on the side of the Mount (jānib aṭ-Ṭūr), and called from the right bank of the valley in 'the blessed spot' (al-buqʿa al-mubāraka). There are no flock and no sandals; the holy ground becomes a blessed spot. nūdiya ... mina sh-shajarati an yā Mūsā innī ana llāhu rabbu l-ʿālamīna ~ wa-yyiqrāʾ ʾēlāyw ʾĕlōhîm mit-tôkh has-səneh wa-yyōʾmer Mōše Mōše ... ʾānōkhî ʾĕlōhê ʾāvîkā: the call from a plant. The bush (səneh) becomes 'the tree' (ash-shajara), the angel in the flame drops out, and 'the God of your father' becomes 'Allāh, Lord of the worlds'.

Only in The golden calf: Aaron builds an altar before the calf and proclaims a feast to YHWH; Intercessor reminds God of his oath to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob; The people eat, drink and rise up to revel before the idol; The prophet's delay on the mountain makes the people lose faith; Whether the calf is a god that leads the people [response between the texts]; The calf is hailed as the god who brought Israel out of Egypt [divergence between the texts]; Israel asks its leader to make them a god [divergence between the texts]; God asks Moses why he hastened ahead of his people to the appointment [divergence between the texts]; The prophet intercedes for the people, arguing from God's reputation; A man called al-Sāmirī leads Israel astray and makes the calf [divergence between the texts]; Aaron's standing before God [divergence between the texts]; Who makes the golden calf and from what [divergence between the texts]; and 7 more.

Only in Exodus, the calf and the wilderness: Israelites who demanded to see God are struck by a thunderbolt and then raised after their death; Who or what parts the sea [divergence between the texts]; Israel's belief or disbelief in Moses after the sea [divergence between the texts]; The cloud over Israel in the wilderness: guide or shade [divergence between the texts]; Longing for fish, cucumbers, melons, leeks, onions and garlic of Egypt; Longing for fish, cucumbers, melons, leeks, onions and garlic of Egypt [divergence between the texts]; The killing of Israelites after the golden calf [divergence between the texts]; Wind brings quail in vast quantity to feed the people [divergence between the texts]; Humans seeing God [contrast between the texts]; People propose appointing a leader to go back to Egypt; Israel told to enter the town's gate prostrating and say 'hitta' (remission); the wrongdoers change the word; Ruler orders the killing of male infants [divergence between the texts]; and 16 more.

leads.summary: These two units share 2 motifs: the killing of israelites after the golden calf [divergence between the texts], the levites kill idolaters including their own kin and are consecrated for it.

passages.note: The killing of Israelites after the golden calf [divergence between the texts] (Exod 32:27 kōh ʾāmar YHWH ʾĕlōhê yiśrāʾēl ... wĕ-hirgû ʾîš ʾet ʾāḥîw: the Levites alone kill about three thousand of their brothers and are ordained for it (32:29 milʾû yedkem ha-yyôm); Q 2:54 fa-tūbū ilā bāriʾikum fa-qtulū anfusakum ... fa-tāba ʿalaykum: the killing is commanded to the whole people as their repentance, and ends in God's forgiveness. leads.summary: These two units share 2 motifs: israel made to drink the golden calf [divergence between the texts], the idol is burned, ground to powder, scattered on water and the people made to drink it.

passages.note: Israel made to drink the golden calf [divergence between the texts] (Exod 32:20 wa-yyiśrōp bā-ʾēš wa-yyiṭḥan ʿad ʾăšer dāq wa-yyizer ʿal pĕnê ha-mmayim wa-yyašq ʾet bĕnê yiśrāʾēl: Moses makes Israel drink the ground-up calf, a physical act; Q 2:93 wa-ushribū fī qulūbihimu l-ʿijla bi-kufrihim 'they were made to drink the calf into their hearts': the same causative 'make drink' (hišqâ / ushribū), now inward, the calf's love soaked into their hearts.)

evidence.text: Confirmed by a side-by-side reading of both originals (alignments/hb-quran/03-hb-quran.yaml): divergence, echo. The calf as if alive: ʿijlan jasadan lahu khuwārun (a body that lows) vs Aaron's wāʾašlikēhû bāʾēš wayyēṣēʾ hāʿēgel hazzeh ('I threw it in the fire and out came this calf'). cf. Pirqe de-R. Eliezer 45 (the calf comes out lowing), outside the canon. Moses returns angry: rajaʿa ... ghaḍbāna asifan; wa-alqā l-alwāḥa vs wayyiḥar ʾap mōšeh wayyašlēk miyyādāw ʾet-hallūḥōt wayšabbēr ʾōtām taḥat hāhār. Q has only 'cast down' (alqā), never 'broke' (Hebrew šibbēr). Moses confronts Aaron, who blames the people: qāla bna umma inna l-qawma staḍʿafūnī wa-kādū yaqtulūnanī vs ʾal-yiḥar ʾap ʾădōnî ʾattāh yādaʿtā ʾet-hāʿām kî bᵉraʿ hûʾ. Changed: in Exod Aaron made the calf and admits throwing the gold into the fire; in Q he is not its maker and pleads that he was overpowered and nearly killed. He also calls Moses 'son of my mother' instead of ʾădōnî 'my lord'; Q adds the violence (akhadha bi-raʾsi akhīhi yajurruhu ilayhi). Punishment for the calf: sa-yanāluhum ghaḍabun min rabbihim wa-dhillatun fī l-ḥayāti d-dunyā vs the Levites' killing of about 3,000 (kišlōšet ʾalpê ʾîš), the deferred visitation (ûbᵉyôm poqdî ûpāqadtî) and the plague (wayyiggōp YHWH ʾet-hāʿām). Q leaves out the Levite slaughter and gives wrath and humiliation in this life. Moses joins himself to the guilty: in Exod in punishment (wᵉʾim-ʾayin mᵉḥēnî nāʾ missiprᵉkā), answered by mî ʾăšer ḥāṭāʾ-lî ʾemḥennû missiprî; in Q in forgiveness (ighfir lī wa-li-akhī; fa-ghfir lanā wa-rḥamnā), answered by inna rabbaka min baʿdihā la-ghafūrun raḥīm for those who repent.

Shared motifs, rarest first: Aaron answers Moses' rebuke over the calf [divergence between the texts] (weight 6.7); How the calf-worshippers are punished [divergence between the texts] (weight 6.7); Moses includes himself with the guilty people in his plea after the calf [divergence between the texts] (weight 6.7); The prophet breaks the tablets in anger at the idolatry (weight 6.3); The idol calf is a body that makes a lowing sound (khuwar) (weight 6.3); What becomes of the first tablets after the calf: broken and replaced, or cast down and taken up again [divergence between the texts] (weight 5.8). Pair score 38.4.

Only in Tablets broken, calf destroyed, Levites slaughter, Moses' offer: Aaron excuses himself: the people pressed him and the calf came out of the fire; The people run wild and become a derision to their enemies; God strikes the people with plague for idolatry; The prophet asks to be blotted from God's book if the people are not forgiven; The noise of the idolatrous revelry is mistaken for the sound of battle; The tablets are written on both sides by God; The leader calls 'Who is for YHWH? To me!' and a group rallies; Calf burned, ground to dust, and the dust thrown into the stream [divergence between the texts]; The calf-maker is condemned to say all his life 'No touching!' (lā misās), an outcast [divergence between the texts]; Israel made to drink the golden calf [divergence between the texts]; God erases what he wills and confirms, and with him is the Mother of the Book (umm al-kitab); God sends an angel ahead of Israel who bears God's name; and 11 more.

Only in The lowing calf and the seventy: Aaron pleads 'son of my mother, the people overpowered me and almost killed me'; The angry prophet seizes his brother by the head (and beard), dragging him; The seventy chosen men are seized by a tremor at the appointed meeting; When his anger subsides the prophet takes up the cast-down tablets again, their text intact; Whether the calf is a god that leads the people [response between the texts]; The people exchanged their Glory for the image of an ox that eats grass; God declares he will be gracious to whom he will be gracious; Moses intercedes for Aaron, with whom God was angry enough to destroy him; God's mercy encompasses all things; Moses prays for Aaron after the calf [divergence between the texts]; Moses 'stood in the breach' (pérets) before God to turn back his wrath from destroying the people; After the calf the people mourn or repent of what they did [divergence between the texts]; and 10 more.

evidence.text: Confirmed by a side-by-side reading of both originals (alignments/hb-quran/04-hb-quran.yaml): divergence, parallel. mah-zzeh bəyādekā wayyōʾmer maṭṭeh, a one-word answer; wa-mā tilka bi-yamīnika yā Mūsā, qāla hiya ʿaṣāya atawakkaʾu ʿalayhā wa-ahushshu bihā ʿalā ghanamī wa-liya fīhā maʾāribu ukhrā. Same question; Q expands Moses' answer into a shepherd's self-portrait. hašlîkēhû ʾarṣâ ... wayhî lənāḥāš wayyānos mōšeh mippānāyw ... šəlaḥ yādəkā weʾĕḥōz bizənābô; alqihā ... fa-idhā hiya ḥayyatun tasʿā, qāla khudhhā wa-lā takhaf sa-nuʿīduhā sīratahā l-ūlā: thrown down, it becomes a snake; he is told to take it and it turns back. Moses flees in Exod; in Q he is told 'do not fear'. Exod: wəhinnēh yādô məṣōraʿat kaššāleg, a leprous hand, given so that the people will believe (ləmaʿan yaʾămînû). Q: takhruj bayḍāʾa min ghayri sūʾ, white 'without harm', which denies the disease, and given li-nuriyaka min āyātinā l-kubrā, a sign for Moses himself. Exod: speech trouble is an objection to the call, lōʾ ʾîš dəbārîm ʾānōkî ... kî kəbad-peh ûkəbad lāšôn ʾānōkî ... šəlaḥ-nāʾ bəyad-tišlāḥ, and God rebukes him, mî śām peh lāʾādām. Q: it is a prayer, rabbi shraḥ lī ṣadrī ... wa-ḥlul ʿuqdatan min lisānī yafqahū qawlī, granted at once, qad ūtīta suʾlaka yā Mūsā. Who initiates, and the mood. Exod: God imposes Aaron in anger, wayyiḥar-ʾap YHWH bəmōšeh ... hălōʾ ʾahărōn ʾāḥîkā ... wəhāyâ-hûʾ yihyeh-ləkā ləpeh wəʾattâ tihyeh-lô lēʾlōhîm. Q: Moses asks for him, wa-jʿal lī wazīran min ahlī Hārūna akhī ushdud bihi azrī wa-ashrikhu fī amrī, so that they may glorify God much (kay nusabbiḥaka kathīrā). No anger, and no 'as God'.

evidence.text: Confirmed by a side-by-side reading of both originals (alignments/hb-quran/05-hb-quran.yaml): divergence, parallel. wa-yaḍīqu ṣadrī wa-lā yanṭaliqu lisānī fa-arsil ilā Hārūna ~ kî khəvad peh û-khəvad lāšôn ʾānōkhî ... šəlaḥ nāʾ bə-yad tišlāḥ: Moses' tongue (lisān / lāšôn) is not free, and he asks God to send someone else. In the Quran he names Aaron himself. God's answer to Moses' reluctance: wa-yyiḥar ʾap YHWH bə-Mōše ... hălōʾ ʾAhărōn ʾāḥîkā ... wə-ʾattâ tihyeh lô lēʾlōhîm (anger; Aaron as mouth, Moses as God to him) ~ qāla kallā fa-dhhabā bi-āyātinā innā maʿakum mustamiʿūna: no anger and no 'as God'; both are sent as equals (fa-dhhabā, dual). Fear of being killed for the old killing: in Exodus God removes it by fact, kî mētû kol hā-ʾănāšîm ham-məvaqšîm ʾet nafšekā; in the Quran Moses raises it himself (wa-lahum ʿalayya dhanbun fa-akhāfu an yaqtulūni), and God answers with his presence, 'kallā ... innā maʿakum mustamiʿūn'. wa-nazaʿa yadahu fa-idhā hiya bayḍāʾu li-n-nāẓirīna ~ wə-hinnēh yādô məṣōraʿat ka-ššāleg: the white hand. In Exodus it is leprous (məṣōraʿat), shown to Moses at the bush and meant for the Israelites (4:8-9, 4:30); in the Quran it is simply 'white for the beholders', shown to Pharaoh and his court, with no disease.

Shared motifs, rarest first: Moses' fear of being killed, on returning, for the Egyptian's death [divergence between the texts] (weight 6.3); Moses' hand turned white as a sign [divergence between the texts] (weight 6.0); Aaron's role beside Moses and how he is appointed [divergence between the texts] (weight 6.0); Prophet's hand turns leprous, white as snow, and is restored as a sign (weight 5.6); Prophet protests he is heavy of mouth and tongue or 'uncircumcised of lips' (weight 5.6); An eloquent brother is appointed to speak for the hero, who is 'as God' to him (weight 5.6); A staff thrown down becomes a serpent and turns back into a staff (weight 5.4). Pair score 40.5.

Only in Signs for Moses, Aaron as mouthpiece, return to Egypt, the bridegroom of blood: Wife saves her husband from a divine attack with her son's circumcision blood, calling him 'bridegroom of blood'; Two brothers meet and kiss at the mountain of God; God attacks the hero at a night lodging and seeks to kill him; God claims to make the mouth, the mute, the deaf, the seeing and the blind; The people believe the prophet's signs and bow in worship; Hero may return home because those seeking his life are dead; Wife cuts off her son's foreskin with a flint and touches it to the threatened man; The hero carries 'the staff of God' with which he performs signs; The prophet asks that his brother be made his helper (wazīr) and partner in his mission [divergence between the texts]; What Moses demands of Pharaoh in God's name [divergence between the texts]; God taught humankind by the pen (qalam) what it did not know; Moses' difficulty of speech, pleaded by himself or thrown at him [divergence between the texts]; and 12 more.

Only in Moses and Pharaoh disputing; the magicians; the sea split like mountains: Pharaoh calls the Israelites 'a small band' who enrage him; God expelled the Egyptians from gardens, springs, treasures and fine dwellings and made Israel inherit them; The magicians cast their spells swearing 'By the might of Pharaoh'; Moses admits he did the killing while he was 'of those astray' and fled out of fear; Pharaoh reproaches Moses: 'Did we not raise you among us as a child, and you did your deed?'; Pharaoh threatens to imprison Moses if he takes a god other than Pharaoh; Before Pharaoh the staff becomes a manifest great serpent (thuʿbān); Prophet's wonders are imitated by the king's magicians in a contest [divergence between the texts]; The title of God in whose name Moses goes to Pharaoh; Egypt reduced the Israelites to slavery; How a public contest between God's prophet and the king's religious specialists ends [contrast between the texts]; The king musters his whole force to pursue the departing people; and 36 more.

leads.summary: These two units share 5 motifs: moses flees from his staff turned serpent, and god's response [divergence between the texts], moses' hand turned white as a sign [divergence between the texts], prophet's hand turns leprous, white as snow, and is restored as a sign, a staff thrown down becomes a serpent and turns back into a staff….

evidence.text: Confirmed by a side-by-side reading of both originals (alignments/hb-quran/05-hb-quran.yaml): divergence. fa-lammā raʾāhā tahtazzu ka-annahā jānnun wallā mudbiran wa-lam yuʿaqqib ~ wa-yhî lə-nāḥāš wa-yyānās Mōše mippānāyw: Moses flees from his transformed staff in both. Exodus then has God order him to grasp the snake by the tail (šəlaḥ yādəkā wə-ʾĕḥōz bi-znāvô); the Quran has God reassure him: yā Mūsā lā takhaf innī lā yakhāfu ladayya l-mursalūna. wa-adkhil yadaka fī jaybika takhruj bayḍāʾa min ghayri sūʾin ~ hāvēʾ nāʾ yādəkā bə-ḥêqekā ... wə-hinnēh yādô məṣōraʿat ka-ššāleg: hand into the bosom (jayb / ḥêq) and out white. The Quran's 'without evil' (min ghayri sūʾ) excludes exactly what Exodus says, that the hand was leprous (məṣōraʿat), and needs no second step of restoring it (4:7).

Shared motifs, rarest first: Moses flees from his staff turned serpent, and God's response [divergence between the texts] (weight 6.3); Moses' hand turned white as a sign [divergence between the texts] (weight 6.0); Prophet's hand turns leprous, white as snow, and is restored as a sign (weight 5.6); A staff thrown down becomes a serpent and turns back into a staff (weight 5.4); The king's heart is hardened (by himself or by God) so he refuses to release the people (weight 4.6). Pair score 27.9.

Only in Signs for Moses, Aaron as mouthpiece, return to Egypt, the bridegroom of blood: Wife saves her husband from a divine attack with her son's circumcision blood, calling him 'bridegroom of blood'; Two brothers meet and kiss at the mountain of God; God attacks the hero at a night lodging and seeks to kill him; God claims to make the mouth, the mute, the deaf, the seeing and the blind; The people believe the prophet's signs and bow in worship; Hero may return home because those seeking his life are dead; Wife cuts off her son's foreskin with a flint and touches it to the threatened man; The hero carries 'the staff of God' with which he performs signs; The prophet asks that his brother be made his helper (wazīr) and partner in his mission [divergence between the texts]; What Moses demands of Pharaoh in God's name [divergence between the texts]; God taught humankind by the pen (qalam) what it did not know; Moses' difficulty of speech, pleaded by himself or thrown at him [divergence between the texts]; and 14 more.

Only in Ta Sin; Moses at the fire, the jann-staff and the nine signs: At the fire the voice proclaims 'Blessed is he who is in the fire and those around it'; God described as the one who dwells in the bush (seneh); How God names himself to Moses from the fire [divergence between the texts]; Moses was given nine clear signs; The number of signs or plagues in Egypt [divergence between the texts]; The thrown staff quivers like a jānn (small snake) and Moses turns and flees without looking back; Why Moses approaches the fire [divergence between the texts]; Traveling with his family, the prophet sees a fire and goes to bring back a brand or find guidance there; God appears in a bush that burns without being consumed; Why Pharaoh and Egypt refuse despite the signs [divergence between the texts]; A poetic list of the Egyptian plagues differs in number and order from Exodus; God addresses the hero with 'Fear not' in a vision; and 2 more.

evidence.text: Confirmed by a side-by-side reading of both originals (alignments/hb-quran/05-hb-quran.yaml): divergence. As at Q 27:10: wa-yyānās Mōše mip-pānāyw ~ wallā mudbiran wa-lam yuʿaqqib; Exodus' command to seize the snake's tail (wə-ʾĕḥōz bi-znāvô) becomes yā Mūsā aqbil wa-lā takhaf innaka mina l-āminīn, 'come forward and do not fear, you are safe'. Two signs, not three, and no leprosy: Exodus gives staff, leprous hand (məṣōraʿat ka-ššāleg), and a third sign held in reserve, Nile water turned to blood (wə-hāyû lə-dām bay-yabbāšet), meant for doubting Israelites; the Quran has fa-dhānika burhānāni min rabbika ilā Firʿawna wa-malaʾihi, two proofs aimed at Pharaoh, the hand white 'without evil' (min ghayri sūʾ), and adds 'draw your arm to your side against fear'. Aaron's eloquence: in Exodus Moses says he is heavy of mouth, and God, angry, proposes Aaron himself: wa-yyiḥar ʾap YHWH bə-Mōše ... yādaʿtî kî dabbēr yədabbēr hûʾ ... wə-śamtā ʾet had-dəvārîm bə-fîw. In the Quran Moses proposes him, wa-akhī Hārūnu huwa afṣaḥu minnī lisānan fa-arsilhu maʿiya ridʾan yuṣaddiqunī, and God agrees without anger: sa-nashuddu ʿaḍudaka bi-akhīka. Aaron is a supporting witness (ridʾ, yuṣaddiqunī), not a mouth for Moses as God. rabbi innī qataltu minhum nafsan fa-akhāfu an yaqtulūni ~ kî mētû kol hā-ʾănāšîm ham-məvaqšîm ʾet nafšekā: the old killing as an obstacle to going back. In Exodus God removes it unasked, in the Quran Moses raises it at the call.

Shared motifs, rarest first: Moses flees from his staff turned serpent, and God's response [divergence between the texts] (weight 6.3); Moses' fear of being killed, on returning, for the Egyptian's death [divergence between the texts] (weight 6.3); Moses' hand turned white as a sign [divergence between the texts] (weight 6.0); Aaron's role beside Moses and how he is appointed [divergence between the texts] (weight 6.0); Prophet's hand turns leprous, white as snow, and is restored as a sign (weight 5.6); Prophet protests he is heavy of mouth and tongue or 'uncircumcised of lips' (weight 5.6); An eloquent brother is appointed to speak for the hero, who is 'as God' to him (weight 5.6); A staff thrown down becomes a serpent and turns back into a staff (weight 5.4). Pair score 46.8.

Only in Signs for Moses, Aaron as mouthpiece, return to Egypt, the bridegroom of blood: Wife saves her husband from a divine attack with her son's circumcision blood, calling him 'bridegroom of blood'; Two brothers meet and kiss at the mountain of God; God attacks the hero at a night lodging and seeks to kill him; God claims to make the mouth, the mute, the deaf, the seeing and the blind; The people believe the prophet's signs and bow in worship; Hero may return home because those seeking his life are dead; Wife cuts off her son's foreskin with a flint and touches it to the threatened man; The hero carries 'the staff of God' with which he performs signs; The prophet asks that his brother be made his helper (wazīr) and partner in his mission [divergence between the texts]; What Moses demands of Pharaoh in God's name [divergence between the texts]; God taught humankind by the pen (qalam) what it did not know; Moses' difficulty of speech, pleaded by himself or thrown at him [divergence between the texts]; and 11 more.

Only in The fire on the side of the Mount; the call from the tree; Aaron as helper: Moses says his brother Aaron is more eloquent of tongue and asks for him as a helper to confirm him; Moses is called from the tree on the right bank of the valley, in the blessed spot; God calls Moses from the fire, from a bush or a tree [divergence between the texts]; Prophet lodges in 'the cave' on Horeb, the mountain of God; Where and how Moses comes to the place of his call [divergence between the texts]; The thrown staff quivers like a jānn (small snake) and Moses turns and flees without looking back; Traveling with his family, the prophet sees a fire and goes to bring back a brand or find guidance there; A shepherd tending flocks comes to the mountain of God and is called; God appears in a bush that burns without being consumed.

passages.note: The divine presence (root sh-k-n / s-k-n) dwelling on the sanctuary or sent down into hearts [divergence between the texts] (Cognate root š-k-n / s-k-n: kî šāḵan ʿālâw he-ʿānān û-ḵəḇôḏ YHWH mālēʾ ʾeṯ ham-miškān (the cloud dwelt on the tent, the glory filled the tabernacle) vs. huwa lladhī anzala s-sakīnata fī qulūbi l-muʾminīna li-yazdādū īmānan (God sent down the sakīna into the believers' hearts). The divine presence dwelling in the sanctuary becomes tranquility sent down into hearts. cf. rabbinic šəḵînâ (later term); the HB has only the verb.)

passages.note: King defies the prophet: 'Who is YHWH that I should obey him?' evidence.text: Confirmed by a side-by-side reading of both originals (alignments/hb-quran/04-hb-quran.yaml): divergence. Title and purpose change. Exod: kōh-ʾāmar YHWH ʾĕlōhê yiśrāʾēl šallaḥ ʾet-ʿammî wəyāḥōggû lî bammidbār ... ʾĕlōhê hāʿibrîm niqrāʾ ʿālênû ... wənizbəḥâ: the God of Israel, of the Hebrews, wants a festival and sacrifice three days into the wilderness. Q: innā rasūlā rabbika, 'messengers of your Lord', Pharaoh's own Lord, and the purpose is release from oppression, fa-arsil maʿanā banī Isrāʾīla wa-lā tuʿadhdhibhum. Q adds wa-s-salāmu ʿalā mani ttabaʿa l-hudā. mî YHWH ʾăšer ʾešmaʿ bəqōlô ... lōʾ yādaʿtî ʾet-YHWH, and Moses gives no answer; fa-man rabbukumā yā Mūsā, and Moses answers with a creation creed, rabbunā lladhī aʿṭā kulla shayʾin khalqahu thumma hadā. Exod's question is about an unknown name; Q's is about a Lord, and the answer is a universal creator. Exod's sequel, the harsher labor (bricks without straw), is left out.

evidence.text: Confirmed by a side-by-side reading of both originals (alignments/hb-quran/02-hb-quran.yaml): divergence, parallel. The magicians' end. Exod: they fail at the lice and say ʾeṣbaʿ ʾĕlōhîm hiwʾ, but stay at court (they are struck by boils at 9:11), and Pharaoh's heart is hardened. Q: wa-ulqiya l-saḥaratu sājidīna qālū āmannā bi-rabbi l-ʿālamīna rabbi Mūsā wa-Hārūna. They convert at the first contest, are threatened with mutilation and crucifixion (la-uqaṭṭiʿanna aydiyakum wa-arjulakum min khilāfin thumma la-uṣallibannakum), and pray to die as muslims (wa-tawaffanā muslimīna). Grudging recognition becomes conversion and martyrdom. Exod: haʿtîrû ʾel-YHWH wə-yāsēr haṣ-ṣəfardəʿîm ... wa-ʾăšalləḥāh ʾet-hā-ʿām, then wa-yyarʾ Parʿōh kî hāyətāh hā-rəwāḥāh wə-hakhbēd ʾet-libbô. Q: yā Mūsā dʿu lanā rabbaka ... la-in kashafta ʿannā l-rijza la-nuʾminanna laka wa-la-nursilanna maʿaka banī Isrāʾīla ... idhā hum yankuthūna. The vow made under a plague and broken afterwards. Q adds a promise of faith (la-nuʾminanna) and says 'they break their word', where Exod says the heart was made heavy.

Shared motifs, rarest first: Magicians fail to imitate a wonder and confess 'This is the finger of God' (weight 6.7); Magicians fail to imitate a wonder and confess 'This is the finger of God' [divergence between the texts] (weight 6.7); The dust of the earth becomes lice on man and beast (weight 6.3); Frogs swarm out of the river into houses, beds, ovens and kneading-troughs (weight 6.0); Nile water is turned to blood (weight 5.8); King asks the prophet to intercede with God to remove a plague (weight 5.6); Prophet delivers God's demand 'Let my people go that they may serve me' (weight 5.4); Prophet's wonders are imitated by the king's magicians in a contest (weight 5.1); The king's heart is hardened (by himself or by God) so he refuses to release the people (weight 4.6). Pair score 52.2.

Only in Plagues 1-3: blood, frogs, lice: The dead frogs are piled in heaps and the land stinks; Egyptians dig around the Nile for drinkable water; Prophet lets the king choose when the plague should end, to prove God's power; The defeated magicians fall prostrate and declare faith in the Lord of Moses and Aaron [divergence between the texts]; How the defeated court magicians respond [divergence between the texts]; The king breaks his promise to release the people once a plague is lifted [divergence between the texts]; Prophet confronts the king at the river in the morning; Why Pharaoh and Egypt refuse despite the signs [divergence between the texts].

Only in Moses before Pharaoh, the magicians and the plagues: Pharaoh's people are struck with years of drought and lack of fruits before the plagues; Enemies attribute their misfortune to the prophet as a bad omen (tatayyur); their omen is with God; The magicians' spell bewitches the people's eyes and terrifies them; The magicians offer the prophet to throw first; he tells them to throw; Pharaoh is said to have his own gods, whom Moses would make him abandon; One of the Egyptian plagues is a flood (tufan); The tyrant threatens to cut off hands and feet on opposite sides and crucify the converts; The king's courtiers advise him how to deal with the prophet and his people [contrast between the texts]; Rulers fear that a people will leave the land, or drive them out of it [divergence between the texts]; The court magicians ask the king for a reward if they win and are promised closeness; Threatened believers say 'to our Lord we return' and pray for patience and to die as muslims; Pharaoh executes or threatens offenders by hanging, impaling or crucifixion; and 16 more.

leads.title: Moses as god to Pharaoh; Aaron's staff becomes a tannin and swallows the magicians' staffs ↔ Moses, the houses as qibla, and Pharaoh's drowning faith
leads.summary: These two units share 5 motifs: who throws the staff before pharaoh and what it becomes, who causes pharaoh's refusal: god hardening his heart, or pharaoh and his people themselves, god sends moses and aaron together, with his signs, to pharaoh, prophet's wonders are imitated by the king's magicians in a contest….

passages.note: Who throws the staff before Pharaoh and what it becomes (The contest with Pharaoh's magicians, with the same verb 'throw' (alqā / hišlîk): qāla lahum mūsā alqū mā antum mulqūn ... inna llāha sa-yubṭiluhu vs wayyašlēk ʾahărōn ʾet-maṭṭēhû ... wayyaʿăśû gam-hēm ḥarṭummê miṣrayim bᵉlahăṭêhem kēn ... wayyiblaʿ maṭṭēh-ʾahărōn ʾet-maṭṭōtām. evidence.text: Confirmed by a side-by-side reading of both originals (alignments/hb-quran/05-hb-quran.yaml): divergence, parallel. Who throws the staff: wa-yyašlēkh ʾAhărōn ʾet maṭṭēhû lifnê Farʿōh ... wa-yhî lə-tannîn ~ fa-alqā ʿaṣāhu fa-idhā hiya thuʿbānun mubīnun, where Moses throws his own staff. The creature: tannîn (sea-dragon or crocodile) ~ thuʿbān (great serpent). Exod 7:11 wa-yyiqrāʾ gam Parʿōh la-ḥăkhāmîm wə-la-mkhaššəfîm, Pharaoh simply summons them and they repeat the sign with their secret arts (bə-lahăṭêhem). The Quran builds a public event: the chiefs advise gathering master sorcerers from all cities, a set day (li-mīqāti yawmin maʿlūm), the people summoned, and the sorcerers bargaining for a reward (a-inna lanā la-ajran). fa-alqā Mūsā ʿaṣāhu fa-idhā hiya talqafu mā yaʾfikūna ~ wa-yyivlaʿ maṭṭēh ʾAhărōn ʾet maṭṭōtām: the prophet's staff swallows the magicians' staffs. The owner differs (Aaron / Moses), and the Quran adds ropes (ḥibālahum) and the oath 'by the might of Pharaoh' (bi-ʿizzati Firʿawn). Pharaoh's response to the sign: Exod 7:13 wa-yyeḥĕzaq lēv Parʿōh wə-lōʾ šāmaʿ ʾălēhem ka-ʾăšer dibber YHWH, the heart hardened as God foretold (God hardens it himself at 14:4, 14:8); Q 26:49 has no hardening and no divine agency, only Pharaoh's rage: āmantum lahu qabla an ādhana lakum innahu la-kabīrukumu lladhī ʿallamakumu s-siḥra, with a threat of amputation and crucifixion.

Shared motifs, rarest first: Prophet's wonders are imitated by the king's magicians in a contest [divergence between the texts] (weight 6.7); Who throws the staff before Pharaoh and what it becomes [divergence between the texts] (weight 6.7); Why Pharaoh and Egypt refuse despite the signs [divergence between the texts] (weight 6.0); The prophet's staff-serpent swallows the magicians' staff-serpents (weight 6.0); An eloquent brother is appointed to speak for the hero, who is 'as God' to him (weight 5.6); A staff thrown down becomes a serpent and turns back into a staff (weight 5.4); Prophet's wonders are imitated by the king's magicians in a contest (weight 5.1). Pair score 41.5.

Only in Moses as god to Pharaoh; Aaron's staff becomes a tannin and swallows the magicians' staffs: Hero is eighty (and his brother eighty-three) when they confront the king; God makes the prophet 'as God' to the king with his brother as his prophet; Wonders done so that Egypt shall know 'I am YHWH'; Pharaoh turned away with his power/pillar (rukn) and called Moses 'a sorcerer or a madman'; Who throws the staff before Pharaoh and what it becomes; An eloquent brother is appointed to speak for the hero, who is 'as God' to him [divergence between the texts]; The prophet's staff-serpent swallows the magicians' staff-serpents [divergence between the texts]; Who causes Pharaoh's refusal: God hardening his heart, or Pharaoh and his people themselves; God sends Moses and Aaron together, with his signs, to Pharaoh; The king's heart is hardened (by himself or by God) so he refuses to release the people [divergence between the texts]; The king's heart is hardened (by himself or by God) so he refuses to release the people.

Only in Moses and Pharaoh disputing; the magicians; the sea split like mountains: Pharaoh calls the Israelites 'a small band' who enrage him; God expelled the Egyptians from gardens, springs, treasures and fine dwellings and made Israel inherit them; The magicians cast their spells swearing 'By the might of Pharaoh'; Moses admits he did the killing while he was 'of those astray' and fled out of fear; Pharaoh reproaches Moses: 'Did we not raise you among us as a child, and you did your deed?'; Pharaoh threatens to imprison Moses if he takes a god other than Pharaoh; Before Pharaoh the staff becomes a manifest great serpent (thuʿbān); The title of God in whose name Moses goes to Pharaoh; Egypt reduced the Israelites to slavery; How a public contest between God's prophet and the king's religious specialists ends [contrast between the texts]; The king musters his whole force to pursue the departing people; Whose forefathers' God is proclaimed in the Moses story [divergence between the texts]; and 36 more.

leads.summary: These two units share 4 motifs: pharaoh acknowledges israel's god or his own sin, and what follows [divergence between the texts], the king confesses he has sinned and that god is righteous, who causes pharaoh's refusal: god hardening his heart, or pharaoh and his people themselves, the king's heart is hardened (by himself or by god) so he refuses to release the people.

passages.note: Pharaoh acknowledges Israel's God or his own sin, and what follows [divergence between the texts] (Pharaoh acknowledges Israel's God: āmantu annahu lā ilāha illā lladhī āmanat bihi banū isrāʾīla wa-ana mina l-muslimīn vs ḥāṭāʾtî happāʿam YHWH haṣṣaddîq waʾănî wᵉʿammî hārᵉšāʿîm. The timing and ending change: in Exod it is in the middle of the plagues, Pharaoh then relapses (wayyōsep laḥăṭōʾ); in Q it is at the moment of drowning (ḥattā idhā adrakahu l-gharaqu), and God refuses it as too late (āl-āna wa-qad ʿaṣayta qablu).)

Shared motifs, rarest first: The beings that carry God's throne, and what they do [divergence between the texts] (weight 6.7); Four living creatures (hayyot) of human form bear the divine throne (weight 6.3). Pair score 13.0.

Only in Ezekiel's inaugural vision by the Chebar canal: four living creatures, wheels full of eyes, the throne and the glory: The heavenly creatures move straight ahead in every direction without turning; The heavenly creatures have straight legs with calves' hooves and human hands under their wings; A firmament gleaming like awesome ice/crystal is spread above the creatures' heads; A vision dated 'in the thirtieth year' without stated era; Fire like torches moves among the creatures and lightning flashes from it; Each heavenly creature has four faces: human, lion, ox and eagle; The center of the fire gleams like hashmal (amber/electrum); The heavens are opened and the prophet sees visions of God; The visionary hedges every description: 'the appearance of the likeness of...'; On the throne is 'a likeness as the appearance of a man'; The prophet is himself a priest or of priestly family; The radiance around the enthroned figure is like the rainbow in the cloud; and 13 more.

Only in Ha-Mim: the Forgiver; the throne-bearers pray for the believers: The damned say 'Lord, you caused us to die twice and gave us life twice; we confess our sins; is there a way out?'; The Day of the Approaching (al-azifa) when hearts reach the throats, choking; God as Forgiver of sin, Accepter of repentance, Severe in punishment, Possessor of bounty (string of divine epithets); God casts the Spirit (al-ruh) of his command upon whom he wills of his servants to warn of the Day of Meeting; God knows the treachery of the eyes and what the breasts conceal; In terror eyes swerve and hearts reach the throats; The angels who bear the Throne and those around it glorify God and ask forgiveness for the believers, praying they and their righteous kin enter Eden; Humans were dead, given life, will die and be given life again (two deaths, two lives); On the Day God asks 'Whose is the kingdom today?' and answers 'God's, the One, the Overpowering'; Formula: 'gracious and merciful, slow to anger, abounding in steadfast love, relenting of evil'; Travel in the land and see the end of those who denied; A surah opens with isolated letters (huruf muqatta'at) of unexplained meaning, e.g. alif-lam-mim.

passages.text: وَٱلْمَلَكُ عَلَىٰٓ أَرْجَآئِهَا وَيَحْمِلُ عَرْشَ رَبِّكَ فَوْقَهُمْ يَوْمَئِذٍ ثَمَٰنِيَةٌ

evidence.text: Confirmed by a side-by-side reading of both originals (alignments/hb-quran/08-hb-quran.yaml): divergence. Throne-bearers: Ezekiel sees ʾarbaʿ ḥayyôt with demût ʾādām, the raqîaʿ over their heads and above it demût kissēʾ with a figure kĕ-marʾēh ʾādām. Q 69:17 wa-l-malaku ʿalā arjāʾihā wa-yaḥmilu ʿarsha rabbika fawqahum yawmaʾidhin thamāniya: EIGHT bear the Throne, at the last day, not in a prophet's vision, and nothing is said of a human likeness on it.

Shared motifs, rarest first: Four living creatures (hayyot) of human form bear the divine throne [divergence between the texts] (weight 6.7); Four living creatures (hayyot) of human form bear the divine throne (weight 6.3). Pair score 13.0.

Only in Ezekiel's inaugural vision by the Chebar canal: four living creatures, wheels full of eyes, the throne and the glory: The heavenly creatures move straight ahead in every direction without turning; The heavenly creatures have straight legs with calves' hooves and human hands under their wings; A firmament gleaming like awesome ice/crystal is spread above the creatures' heads; A vision dated 'in the thirtieth year' without stated era; Fire like torches moves among the creatures and lightning flashes from it; Each heavenly creature has four faces: human, lion, ox and eagle; The center of the fire gleams like hashmal (amber/electrum); The heavens are opened and the prophet sees visions of God; The visionary hedges every description: 'the appearance of the likeness of...'; On the throne is 'a likeness as the appearance of a man'; The prophet is himself a priest or of priestly family; The radiance around the enthroned figure is like the rainbow in the cloud; and 13 more.

Only in Al-Haqqa: Thamud and 'Ad, the running ship, the single trumpet blast, the sky split and eight bearing the Throne: 'Ad were destroyed by a furious wind for seven nights and eight days, lying felled like hollow palm trunks; When the water overflowed God carried 'you' in the running ship (al-jariya) as a reminder for retaining ears; That day eight (angels) bear the Throne of your Lord above them; At a single blast on the trumpet, the earth and mountains are lifted and crushed with a single crushing; Thamud were destroyed by the Overwhelming (al-tagiya, the Blast); Rhetorical opening: 'The Reality (al-haqqa)! What is the Reality? And what will make you know what the Reality is?'; When the water overflowed God carried 'you' in the running ship (al-jariya) as a reminder for retaining ears [divergence between the texts]; The overturned city (al-mu'tafika, Sodom) God hurled down and covered with what covered it; A roaring cold wind (sarsar) on a day of continuous ill omen plucks men away like trunks of uprooted palms; The sky splits and is frail that day, and the angels are on its borders; When the Event (al-waqi'a) befalls, none can deny it: it abases and exalts; Cities overturned (hafakh) and the plain destroyed; and 3 more.

Al-Haqqa: Thamud and 'Ad, the running ship, the single trumpet blast, the sky split and eight bearing the Throne: tagged by Claude (model), reading the Arabic.

Only in The cauldron saying, death of Pelatiah, God as little sanctuary, the new heart, the glory on the Mount of Olives: A man dies suddenly while the prophet is still prophesying against him; Proverb 'the city is the cauldron and we are the meat', turned against its speakers; God himself becomes 'a little sanctuary' (miqdash me'at) for the exiles in the lands of dispersion; The spirit carries the prophet back to the exiles and the vision lifts from him; Prophet falls on his face crying 'Ah Lord, will you destroy the whole remnant of Israel?'; The divine glory leaves the temple in stages: from the cherub to the threshold, to the east gate, to the mountain east of the city; Formula 'and you/they shall know that I am YHWH' closing a judgment or salvation oracle; God will gather the dispersed from the peoples and give them back the land of Israel; Formula 'I will take you as my people and I will be your God'.

Only in The cow and the slain man: Moses commands a cow be slaughtered; the people repeatedly ask its age, color and nature before complying; Hearts harder than stones, yet some stones gush rivers, split for water or fall down in fear of God; A slain man is struck with part of the slaughtered cow and revived to reveal his killer; The sacrificial cow is bright yellow, pleasing to beholders; What contact with a corpse does [contrast between the texts]; Unyoked milk cows pull a new cart unguided, separated from their calves, as a divine test; Description of the cow required by God [divergence between the texts]; A heifer and a killing whose perpetrator is unknown [divergence between the texts]; Unblemished red cow never yoked is burned whole for purifying ash; Unsolved murder: elders of nearest city break the neck of an unworked heifer in an untilled wadi.

Only in Fire in the southern forest; the song of the sword; Babylon's divination at the crossroads; against Ammon: God kindles an unquenchable fire in the forest of the south that devours every green tree and every dry tree; Divination by inspecting the liver (hepatoscopy); At the fork of two roads the king of Babylon divines: he shakes arrows, consults teraphim and inspects the liver; Prophet commanded to groan with breaking loins before the people; when asked why, he announces coming news; 'A ruin, a ruin, a ruin I will make it ... until he comes to whom judgment belongs, and I will give it to him'; Incantatory song of the sharpened and polished sword, flashing like lightning, given to the slayer; God draws his sword from its sheath against righteous and wicked alike, and it will not return; The sword is returned to its sheath and Ammon is judged in the land of its origin and forgotten; Remove the turban and take off the crown: the low exalted, the high brought low; Divination by shaking or drawing arrows (belomancy); In terror all hands go slack and all knees run with water; Scepter shall not depart from Judah until Shiloh comes and peoples obey him; and 4 more.

Only in The plot against the prophet and the worship of the pagans: Fight them until there is no persecution (fitna) and religion is wholly God's; If unbelievers desist, what is past is forgiven; God separates the bad from the good, heaps the bad on one another and casts them into hell; Deniers pray: 'If this is the truth from you, rain stones on us from the sky'; God will not punish a people while the prophet is among them or while they seek forgiveness; The pagans' prayer at the House was only whistling and clapping; Whether the righteous among a guilty people shield it from punishment [contrast between the texts]; Hero bargains with God to spare a city for the sake of a few righteous (50 down to 10); God's plotting (makr / kayd) outwits the schemers; none is safe from it but the losers; Unbelievers plot to confine, kill or expel the prophet, but God plots too; Deniers dare the prophet: 'Bring us what you threaten, if you are truthful'; Unbelievers dismiss the revelation as 'tales of the ancients' (asatir al-awwalin) they could equal.

evidence.text: Confirmed by a side-by-side reading of both originals (alignments/hb-quran/07-hb-quran.yaml): parallel. Pharaoh's boast of owning the Nile channels: hat-tannîm hag-gāḏôl hā-rōḇēṣ bə-ṯôḵ yəʾōrâw ʾăšer ʾāmar lî yəʾōrî wa-ʾănî ʿăśîṯinî vs. yā qawmi a-laysa lī mulku miṣra wa-hādhihi l-anhāru tajrī min taḥtī. Ezekiel's Pharaoh claims to have made himself (or the Nile); the Quran's claims kingship and the rivers. Neither boast is in Exodus.

Shared motifs, rarest first: Pharaoh boasts to his people: is not the kingdom of Egypt mine, and these rivers flowing beneath me? (weight 6.7); Pharaoh is the great tannin (crocodile/dragon) lying in the midst of his Nile channels (weight 6.7). Pair score 13.4.

Only in Pharaoh the great dragon of the Nile; Egypt as a reed; Egypt given as Nebuchadnezzar's wages: Nebuchadnezzar's army labored at Tyre till every head was bald and shoulder rubbed, without reward, so God gives him Egypt as wages; God puts hooks in the monster's jaws, makes the fish of its rivers stick to its scales and hauls it out of the water; On that day God will make a horn sprout for the house of Israel; Pharaoh boasts 'My Nile is my own; I made it (or made myself)'; God gives the prophet 'an opening of the mouth' among the people; Egypt will be desolate forty years, uninhabited from Migdol to Syene and the border of Cush, then restored to Pathros as a lowly kingdom; Egypt's extent 'from Migdol to Syene (Aswan) and the border of Cush'; Can you draw out Leviathan with a hook, put a cord in his nose, make him a pet or a slave forever?; The hauled-out monster is flung into the wilderness on the open field as food for beasts and birds, unburied; Pharaoh tells his chiefs: 'I know of no god for you other than me'; Pharaoh gathers the people and proclaims 'I am your Lord most high'; Egypt likened to a broken reed staff that pierces the hand of whoever leans on it; and 3 more.

Only in Moses before Pharaoh: the laughing courtiers, the rivers beneath Pharaoh and the drowning: Each sign shown to Pharaoh's people was greater than the one before it; Pharaoh scorns Moses as contemptible, barely able to speak, without gold bracelets or attending angels; The king's courtiers advise him how to deal with the prophet and his people [divergence between the texts]; The title of God in whose name Moses goes to Pharaoh [divergence between the texts]; Moses' difficulty of speech, pleaded by himself or thrown at him [divergence between the texts]; The king breaks his promise to release the people once a plague is lifted [divergence between the texts]; Who causes Pharaoh's refusal: God hardening his heart, or Pharaoh and his people themselves [divergence between the texts]; The returning waters drown the pursuing army; not one survives [divergence between the texts]; King invests the hero with ring, linen and chariot; The king breaks his promise to release the people once a plague is lifted; Prophet protests he is heavy of mouth and tongue or 'uncircumcised of lips'; Prophet's wonders are imitated by the king's magicians in a contest; and 1 more.

Ezek 36:26 wa-hăsirōtî ʾet lēb hā-ʾeben mi-bbĕśarkem wĕ-nātattî lākem lēb bāśār: God will take away the heart of stone; Q 2:74 thumma qasat qulūbukum min baʿdi dhālika fa-hiya ka-l-ḥijārati aw ashaddu qaswatan: the hearts became like stone or harder, and stones are said to be better: some gush water, split, or fall in fear of God. Promise of a new heart vs indictment of hearts harder than rock.
Shared motifs, rarest first: Hearts of stone [divergence between the texts] (weight 6.3); God will remove the heart of stone and give a heart of flesh and a new spirit (weight 5.8). Pair score 12.1.

Only in For my holy name - clean water, new heart, my spirit within; the land like Eden: Onlookers say 'This desolate land has become like the garden of Eden'; The exiles profane God's holy name among the nations, who say 'These are YHWH's people, yet they had to leave his land'; Israel's conduct defiled the land 'like the uncleanness of a menstruous woman'; God will multiply the people like flocks of men, like the holy flocks of Jerusalem at her appointed feasts; God declares 'Not for your sake do I act, O house of Israel, but for my holy name which you profaned'; God will sprinkle clean water upon them and purify them from all their uncleanness and idols; God will put his own spirit within them and cause them to walk in his statutes; The people's hearts are called hard (Arabic q-s-w, Hebrew q-sh-h), or God makes them so [divergence between the texts]; The land is impure with the impurity (niddah) of its peoples, filled from end to end; Survivors in exile will remember God, loathe themselves for their abominations and know he did not speak in vain; God is to be sanctified in the midst of Israel; his holy name not profaned; God will gather the dispersed from the peoples and give them back the land of Israel; and 1 more.

Only in The cow and the slain man: Moses commands a cow be slaughtered; the people repeatedly ask its age, color and nature before complying; Hearts harder than stones, yet some stones gush rivers, split for water or fall down in fear of God; A slain man is struck with part of the slaughtered cow and revived to reveal his killer; The sacrificial cow is bright yellow, pleasing to beholders; What contact with a corpse does [contrast between the texts]; Unyoked milk cows pull a new cart unguided, separated from their calves, as a divine test; Description of the cow required by God [divergence between the texts]; A heifer and a killing whose perpetrator is unknown [divergence between the texts]; Unblemished red cow never yoked is burned whole for purifying ash; Unsolved murder: elders of nearest city break the neck of an unworked heifer in an untilled wadi.

leads.title: The valley of dry bones ↔ Daughters of God, all things glorify him, bones and dust, the cursed tree (Surah 17:40-60)
leads.summary: These two units share 1 motifs: deniers ask 'when we are bones and fragments, shall we be raised as a new creation?'.

passages.note: Deniers ask 'When we are bones and fragments, shall we be raised as a new creation?' (hătiḥyênâ hāʿăṣāmôt hāʾēlleh ... yābəšû ʿaṣmôtênû wəʾābədâ tiqwātēnû; a-idhā kunnā ʿiẓāman wa-rufātan a-innā la-mabʿūthūna khalqan jadīdā: can dry bones (ʿăṣāmôt / ʿiẓām, cognate) live again? Ezek's doubters are the exiles in despair, and the bones are a figure for national restoration. Q's doubters are deniers mocking, and the answer is literal: alladhī faṭarakum awwala marra.)

Shared motifs, rarest first: Deniers ask 'When we are bones and fragments, shall we be raised as a new creation?' (weight 5.4). Pair score 5.4.

Only in The valley of dry bones: God will open his people's graves, bring them up from their graves and bring them to the land of Israel; The exiles say 'Our bones are dried up, our hope is lost, we are cut off'; The prophet summons the breath (ruah) from the four winds to breathe into the slain so they live; The prophet is set down in a valley full of very many, very dry bones and led around among them; In the womb God makes the lump into bones and clothes the bones with flesh, then makes it another creation; God asks 'Can these bones live?' and the prophet answers 'Lord God, you know'; The revived dead stand on their feet, an exceedingly great army; God will put his own spirit within them and cause them to walk in his statutes; A multitude of dead revived [divergence between the texts]; The question whether God can make the dead live [divergence between the texts]; The question whether dead bones can live again, and who asks it [divergence between the texts]; A single cry or rebuke (zajra) and the dead stand looking; and 3 more.

Only in Daughters of God, all things glorify him, bones and dust, the cursed tree (Surah 17:40-60): Answer to the deniers: even if you were stone or iron, the one who made you first will raise you; Every town will be destroyed or severely punished before the Day of Resurrection, as inscribed in the Book; Those whom the polytheists invoke themselves seek a means (wasila) of nearness to God; When the prophet recites, God places a hidden veil between him and those who deny the hereafter; The prophet's vision and the cursed tree in the Quran are made a trial for people; 'Let everything that has breath (neshamah) praise Yah'; 'Let everything that has breath (neshamah) praise Yah' [divergence between the texts]; If there were other gods they would seek a way to the Lord of the Throne; Opponents say the believers follow only a bewitched man (rajul mashur); Satan stirs up enmity (nazagha) between brothers or among people; Thamud's most wretched one rises; the messenger warns 'God's she-camel and her drinking'; they hamstring her and God crushes them; The seven heavens, the earth and everything in them glorify God, though humans do not understand their praise; and 6 more.

evidence.text: Confirmed by a side-by-side reading of both originals (alignments/hb-quran/01-hb-quran.yaml): divergence, parallel. Ezek 37:3 ha-tiḥyênâ hā-ʿăṣāmôt hā-ʾēlleh wā-ʾōmar ʾădōnāy YHWH ʾattâ yādāʿtā: God asks if the bones can live and the prophet defers to God's knowledge; Q 2:259 qāla annā yuḥyī hādhihi llāhu baʿda mawtihā: the man himself asks, doubting, how God can revive the dead town, and God answers by making him die for a hundred years and raising him. Ezek 37:7-8 wa-ttiqrĕbû ʿăṣāmôt ʿeṣem ʾel ʿaṣmô ... wĕ-hinnēh ʿălêhem gīdîm û-bāśār ʿālâ wa-yyiqram ʿălêhem ʿôr: bones come together and are covered with sinews, flesh and skin; Q 2:259 wa-nẓur ilā l-ʿiẓāmi kayfa nunshizuhā thumma naksūhā laḥman: see the bones, how we raise them up and then clothe them with flesh. Same order (assemble, then cover with flesh); in the Quran they are the man's donkey's bones and the sign is for one doubter, not a vision of the nation.

Shared motifs, rarest first: The question whether God can make the dead live [divergence between the texts] (weight 6.7); At the prophet's word there is a rattling; bones come together bone to bone, then sinews, flesh and skin cover them, but there is no breath (weight 6.3). Pair score 13.0.

Only in The valley of dry bones: God will open his people's graves, bring them up from their graves and bring them to the land of Israel; The exiles say 'Our bones are dried up, our hope is lost, we are cut off'; The prophet summons the breath (ruah) from the four winds to breathe into the slain so they live; The prophet is set down in a valley full of very many, very dry bones and led around among them; In the womb God makes the lump into bones and clothes the bones with flesh, then makes it another creation; God asks 'Can these bones live?' and the prophet answers 'Lord God, you know'; The revived dead stand on their feet, an exceedingly great army; God will put his own spirit within them and cause them to walk in his statutes; A multitude of dead revived [divergence between the texts]; The question whether dead bones can live again, and who asks it [divergence between the texts]; A single cry or rebuke (zajra) and the dead stand looking; Deniers ask 'When we are bones and fragments, shall we be raised as a new creation?'; and 2 more.

Only in The man who passed a ruined town: The sleeper is shown his donkey's bones assembled and clothed with flesh; After a century the sleeper's food and drink have not spoiled; A man passing a ruined town is made to die for a hundred years, then revived, thinking he slept a day or part of a day; A destroyed city is made a perpetual ruin-mound (tel olam); The fate of a destroyed town: lasting ruin or revival [contrast between the texts].

Only in Gog of Magog invades the land dwelling at the navel of the earth: The invader plots to attack a quiet people dwelling securely in unwalled villages without bars or gates, to seize plunder; Gog's coalition: Persia, Cush, Put, Gomer with all its hordes, Beth-togarmah from the far north, many peoples; God asks 'Are you the one of whom I spoke in former days through my servants the prophets?'; God turns the invader around and puts hooks in his jaws to drag him out with all his army; The invading host comes up like a storm, like a cloud covering the land; Every man's sword is turned against his brother in the enemy host; Gog is summoned 'after many days', 'in the latter years / end of days', against a land restored from the sword; Restored Israel dwells 'on the navel of the earth' (tabbur ha-arets); God judges Gog with pestilence, blood, torrential rain, hailstones, fire and sulfur; Sheba, Dedan and the merchants of Tarshish ask the invader 'Have you come to take plunder?'; Gog of the land of Magog, chief prince (nesi rosh) of Meshech and Tubal, an eschatological invader [divergence between the texts]; The final invader comes from the farthest recesses of the north (yarketei tsafon); and 9 more.

Q: no battle is told; the release of Gog and Magog leads directly to the trumpet and the gathering (wa-nufikha fī ṣ-ṣūr ... wa-ʿaraḍnā jahannama). An end-time invasion becomes a sign of the Hour.

Shared motifs, rarest first: Gog and Magog are let loose and swarm down from every height before the end [divergence between the texts] (weight 6.0); Gog of the land of Magog, chief prince (nesi rosh) of Meshech and Tubal, an eschatological invader (weight 6.0). Pair score 12.0.

Only in Gog's fall, seven years of burning weapons, the Valley of Hamon-Gog and the great feast of the birds: God strikes the bow from the invader's left hand and makes the arrows drop from his right hand; The nations will know that Israel went into exile for its own iniquity because God hid his face, not because he was weak; The carrion-eaters are sated at God's table with horses, charioteers, warriors and all men of war; God sends fire on Magog and on those who dwell securely in the coastlands; God will no longer hide his face from Israel, for he has poured out his spirit on the house of Israel; Israel plunders those who plundered them and despoils those who despoiled them; God invites every bird and beast to his great sacrifice on the mountains of Israel to eat the flesh of mighty men and drink the blood of princes, as of rams, lambs, goats and Bashan bulls, till drunk with blood; All Israel buries the dead for seven months to purify the land; appointed men search the land and mark every human bone with a sign (tsiyyun) for the buriers; Gog and his horde are buried in the Valley of the Travelers east of the sea, renamed Valley of Hamon-Gog; a city is named Hamonah; Israel's townsfolk burn the enemy weapons (shields, bows, arrows, clubs, spears) as fuel for seven years, cutting no wood from the forest; Strong bulls of Bashan encircle the sufferer; Slain enemies become a portion for jackals or food for beasts and birds; and 6 more.

Only in Dhul-Qarnayn, the setting and rising sun, and the barrier against Gog and Magog (Surah 18:83-101): When God's promise comes the barrier is leveled to the ground; The conqueror is given the choice to punish the people at the sunset or treat them kindly; A people complain that Gog and Magog spread corruption in the land; A barrier of iron blocks filling the gap between two cliffs, heated with bellows and sealed with molten copper, shuts out Gog and Magog; At the sun's rising the conqueror finds a people with no shelter from it; Between two mountain barriers the conqueror finds a people who scarcely understand speech; At the end peoples surge into one another like waves; At the place of sunset the conqueror finds the sun setting in a muddy (or hot) spring; The people offer tribute for a barrier; the conqueror declines payment and asks for their labor; Gog and Magog are let loose and swarm down from every height before the end; Gog of the land of Magog, chief prince (nesi rosh) of Meshech and Tubal, an eschatological invader [divergence between the texts]; Dhu l-Qarnayn ('the two-horned') is given power on earth and a way to everything; and 2 more.
